intuition.text: The mapper is the one piece of code that knows both shapes: how a composition is written down in storage, and what the scene needs of one in memory. step0.title: Find through the identity map
step0.text: The scene asks the mapper, never storage, for a composition. One the mapper has built before comes straight from its identity map without a read, so the scene holds a single object for each composition however often it asks. Rows read so far: {reads}.

step1.title: Map a row into an object
step1.text: To build a composition the mapper checks the row's format and decodes its steps; the object it makes has no format, no storage key and no way to save itself. A row in a format it does not read stands for no object: it is noted as unmapped and left exactly as it is. Objects in the identity map: {mapped}.

step2.title: Change the object, not the row
step2.text: Renaming is domain work on the object. No storage code runs, so for a while the object is ahead of its row, and only the mapper can bring the two together again.

step3.title: Write the object's own row
step3.text: update builds a row from the object, in the format this build writes, and replaces that row and no other. Writes to storage so far: {writes}.

step4.title: Leave alone what could not be read
step4.text: Since every write names one row, a row the mapper could not map is never written over. A save that writes the whole library as one value cannot keep that promise: it builds the value from the objects it holds, so an unmapped row is simply not in it. Rows in storage now: {rows}.

pseudocode.ordinary:
find(id):
  if id in identityMap:
    return identityMap[id]
  reads = reads + 1
  return load(id, storage.read(id))

load(id, row):
  if row.format != formatRead:
    unmapped.add(id)
    return none
  composition = new Composition(row.title, decodeSteps(row.steps))
  identityMap[id] = composition
  return composition

composition.rename(title):
  composition.title = title

update(composition):
  id = identityMap.keyOf(composition)
  row = { format: formatRead, title: composition.title, steps: encodeSteps(composition.steps) }
  storage.write(id, row)

save(changed):
  for composition in changed:
    update(composition)
saveAll():
  storage.writeAll(rowsOf(identityMap))   // no row for an unmapped id, so its stored row is lost

limits.item0: Choose the whole library (0), the way the app's scene store saves, and step to the save: the library goes back to storage as one value built from the objects in the identity map, and Dawn patrol, which the mapper could not read, has no object, so its row is gone. limits.item1: Format drift never ends. A mapper that reads only the newest format cannot read old rows, and an old build cannot read new ones, so a store that lives across releases needs a mapper that reads every format it has ever written, or a migration that rewrites the rows before the new build reads them. Set Dawn patrol's row format to {formatRead} and the trouble goes away only because both builds now agree.
limits.item2: The mapper has to read and set every field it maps, so the domain object either exposes them or lets the mapper reach past its constructor, as MikroORM does when it restores a stored entity. Whatever the constructor would have checked is then not checked on load, and a row that decodes cleanly but breaks a rule becomes an object that breaks it too.
limits.item3: The identity map promises one object per row only inside one mapper. Each tab has its own, so a rename in one is invisible to the other until it reads the row again, and when both save, the later write wins; a version kept on the row and checked at the save is what catches that.
limits.item4: When the stored shape already is the domain's shape, as the app's compositions are, a hand-written mapper is code that copies fields one to one. The pattern earns its cost where the shapes differ, or must stay free to differ, and with many classes a mapper driven by a description of fields and columns keeps that cost down.

intuition.text: Inside the server, an actor definition simply holds its saved build, and the build holds the actors that use it. A network carries none of that: only bytes cross, so whatever the server sends must be data alone, each object copied and each reference turned into an id, with nothing in it that needs the server to make sense of it. A Data Transfer Object is that copy made on purpose: shaped for the call that carries it, naming its own format so that the reader can tell whether it understands it, and filled by an assembler, the only code that knows both the server's objects and the shape on the wire. It is the other half of a Remote Facade: the facade makes one call do the work of many, and the transfer object is what that one call carries.
intuition.situation: The board page asks the app's API for the whole board in one call. The answer must hold every panel, row, cell and evidence entry the page may show, in a form JSON can carry and the page can check before it trusts it. The uifa-board-v1 document the app already reads is that form; this study follows three of the objects behind it from the server's memory to the page's view.

example.name: The board's reply, copied for the trip
example.description: The board's reply carries three of the server's objects: an actor definition, the saved build it points at, which has {buildSteps} steps, and the evidence record it cites. On the server they hold each other, and the build lists the actor back. The author's assembler copies them into a sketch of the uifa-board-v1 document, written as version {serverVersion}, and the page reads it knowing version {pageVersion}. The page's side follows the app's code; the server's side is the author's sketch, since in this repository a mock serves a recorded document.

step0.title: Start from the domain objects
step0.text: On the server the objects refer to each other directly: the actor holds its build and its evidence, and the build holds the actor. Encoding that graph as it stands fails on the cycle, and even without one it would carry every field the server keeps and tie the page to the server's classes.

step1.title: Copy each object, references as ids
step1.text: The assembler copies one object at a time into the DTO. Each reference becomes the id of what it points at: the actor's build becomes a link to the build's row, and its evidence the evidence record's id. The build's list of users is not copied, so the DTO links one way and has no cycle.

step2.title: Encode once, with the version
step2.text: The whole DTO is serialised as one text that names its own format, and sent as the reply to the one call; the text on the wire: {encoded}. Nothing in it needs the server to be read.

step3.title: Check the version, then read
step3.text: The page parses the text and reads it only if it names the version the page knows, version {pageVersion}. The page's own assembler then turns the DTO into its view, resolving each link against the rows the document holds. The page never sees the server's classes, and the server never sees the page's view.

pseudocode.ordinary:
actor = definitions.find("definition-1")
// actor.build is the saved build, and actor.build.usedBy holds actor again
json.encode(actor)   // refused: the graph has a cycle

assemble(actor):
  dto = { panels: { actors: [], builds: [] }, evidence: [] }
  dto.panels.actors.add({ id: actor.id,
    cells: [{ key: "kind", value: actor.kind, evidence: idsOf(actor.evidence) }],
    links: [{ target: actor.build.id }] })
  dto.panels.builds.add({ id: actor.build.id,
    cells: [{ key: "steps", value: actor.build.steps }] })   // usedBy is left behind
  for record in actor.evidence: dto.evidence.add({ id: record.id, source: record.source })
  return dto

text = json.encode({ viewModelVersion: "uifa-board-v" + serverVersion, ...assemble(actor) })
reply(text)

document = json.decode(text)
if document.viewModelVersion != "uifa-board-v" + pageVersion:
  show the unsupported-version notice; stop
view.targets = { row.id: panel for each row of each panel in document }
view.links = [link for each row's links if link.target in view.targets]

item1.relevance: MikroORM is a TypeScript object-relational mapper; its serializer turns managed entities into plain objects ready to send, the step an assembler performs.
item1.explanation: serialize() walks an entity's properties and writes a plain object. A related entity not named in populate is written as its primary key, or as an object holding only the key when forceObject is set; a collection that was never loaded is left out rather than loaded; exclude, fields and serialisation groups hide what a client should not see; and it records the entities it has visited, so that a cycle is not followed round again. Its output is a generic DTO derived from the entity's metadata rather than a class written for one screen, so the shape on the wire still follows the entity.

limits.item0: The two sides agree only through the version. Set the server's version to 2 and step to the decode: the page knows version {pageVersion}, finds a version it does not know and refuses the whole document, as the board shows its unsupported-version notice. Without that check, version 2's renamed field would read as missing, and the actor would arrive with no cells and nothing to say why.
limits.item1: A DTO is a copy, out of date the moment it is encoded. Nothing ties the text to the objects it came from, so a build saved again on the server after the reply leaves the page showing the old step count until the page loads the board again.
limits.item2: An id is useful only if what it names travelled too. The actor's link resolves because its build is in the same document; a link to a row the document left out cannot be followed, and the board draws such a link marked target unavailable. Shaping a DTO for one use case means deciding which neighbours come with it.
limits.item3: Every field is written twice, once where the assembler fills the DTO and once where the reader takes it apart, and the two must change together. One DTO per screen multiplies that mapping; a generic one, such as a record set or a map of fields, saves it but gives up the types that made the contract checkable. Inside one process a DTO only adds a copy: pass the objects themselves.

intuition.text: Organise the code by the things it handles rather than by the requests made of it. A composition, a step and the scene each own the rules about themselves, and a request becomes a short conversation among them. The rule that a step stays within the engine's bounds is written once, on the step, so every request that makes a step obeys it without having to remember; a rule that differs by kind of step is a method each kind answers in its own way, not a branch in every procedure that handles steps. The cost is a second structure to keep in step with the first: objects whose shape is not the stored shape, and a mapper between them. This app made the opposite choice, readonly interfaces for its data and pure functions for its rules, so this study's example is a design the app does not have.
intuition.situation: The soldier scene takes compositions in from three places: the save, which builds one from the run; the saved list, read back from browser storage when the page loads; and text that someone exported. If a composition could only come into being through its own constructor, and only the scene could take one in, every one of those paths would get every check the composition and the scene define, the scene check included, without any of them listing the checks. A colleague adding a fourth path, such as duplicating a saved composition, would inherit the same checks without being told about them.

example.name: Importing an exported composition, as objects
example.description: The same paste into the soldier scene's import box, written as a domain model the app does not have. Composition.fromExport reads the text and makes each step with Step.from, which picks a class by the step's kind: an objective step, which needs no units, or a step that acts on units and needs at least one. A step refuses to exist outside the engine's bounds. The scene then admits the composition only if it was made in this scene, and replays it. Reading the saved list back from browser storage goes through the same constructors and the same admit, so it is held to every rule an import is.

step0.title: Give each rule an owner
step0.text: A composition answers for its own fields, a step for staying inside the engine's bounds, and the scene for what belongs to it. Nothing else checks those rules, so each has one place to be read or changed.

step1.title: Build through constructors that refuse
step1.text: Composition.fromExport parses the text, checks the export tag and makes every step with Step.from, and the constructor refuses a missing or mistyped field. A composition that exists has passed every check of its own and of its steps, so code that is handed one need not check it again.

step2.title: Let each kind answer for itself
step2.text: Step.from picks a class by the step's kind. Whether a step needs units is a method each class answers: an objective step says no, the others yes. A new kind with a rule of its own is a new class, and the code that replays steps does not change.

step3.title: Admit through the scene
step3.text: admit is the scene's only way in: opening an import and restoring the saved list both pass through it, and it refuses a composition made in another scene. A rule written there binds every path that brings a composition, including paths not yet written.

step4.title: Keep the service thin and map at the edges
step4.text: Each request becomes a line that asks the objects to act. A mapper turns the objects into the plain JSON that browser storage holds and back again, building through the same constructors, so a stored composition is held to the rules an imported one is.

pseudocode.ordinary:
// each rule has one owner, and only its owner checks it
class Composition   // owns: its fields are whole
class Step          // owns: it stays inside the engine's bounds
class Scene         // owns: what belongs to it

Composition.fromExport(text):
  value = parseJson(text), or refuse if it does not parse
  if value.schema != exportSchema: refuse
  steps = each record in value.composition.steps, made by Step.from
  return new Composition(value.composition, steps)
  // the constructor refuses a missing or mistyped field

Step.from(record):
  if record.at > lastFrame: refuse
  if a parameter is beyond largestNumber or below its least value: refuse
  if record.kind is the objective kind: return new ObjectiveStep(record)
  return new UnitStep(record)
ObjectiveStep.needsUnits(): false
UnitStep.needsUnits(): true

Scene.admit(composition):              // the only way into a scene
  if composition.sceneId != this.id: refuse
  return composition
Scene.open(composition):
  c = this.admit(composition)
  replay c.steps from c.seed, refusing a step
    whose needsUnits() is true when it selects no unit
Scene.restore(compositions):
  keep each composition that this.admit accepts

importJson(text):                      // the service: a line per request
  scene.open(Composition.fromExport(text))
reload(stored):
  scene.restore(each stored record, made by CompositionMapper.fromStored)
save():
  storage.write(each of scene's compositions, made by CompositionMapper.toStored)
// fromStored builds through the same constructors, so it meets the same rules

item0.explanation: The author's reading of the code, not a claim that it was designed as this pattern, and in most respects it is the opposite choice. The engine's things, a unit, a formation, a step of a composition, are readonly interfaces in types.ts with no methods, and every rule is a pure function from one state to the next. It shares one aim with a domain model: its logic is arranged by the domain's things, in steering, formation and slot-assignment modules, not by the page's requests, and its interpreters table gives each step kind a function of its own, which is how a function-first codebase does what a domain model does with a subclass per kind. It stops there. refusalOf still asks whether a step is the objective kind to decide whether it needs units; applyStep does not call isSafeStep, which runs only when a composition is read from storage or from an export, so the bounds are the reader's rule rather than the step's; and with no objects there is no mapping layer to keep, because a composition is already the shape it is stored in.

item1.relevance: Doctrine ORM is an object-relational mapper for PHP, and its own tutorial argues for entities that carry the domain's behaviour, which is this pattern's central choice.
item1.explanation: The tutorial sets out two ways to write an entity: with getters and setters, which it calls anemic and which leave the business logic in services, or with methods named for business operations, which it calls rich and recommends, because an entity that changes only after checking its own invariants cannot be left in an invalid state and then flushed to the database. It also says why Doctrine can afford that: it reads and writes an entity's fields by reflection and never calls its methods, not even its constructor, so the class is free to make construction strict. That is the mapping layer a domain model needs, kept out of the domain classes by a data mapper.

item2.relevance: MikroORM is a TypeScript object-relational mapper whose entities are classes, and its inheritance mapping is what lets a domain model keep a subclass for each kind of thing through a relational database.
item2.explanation: With single table inheritance every class in a hierarchy shares one table, and a discriminator column, mapped value by value to classes, decides which class each row is loaded as; columns that only a subclass has must allow null. With table-per-type inheritance each class has its own table, an insert writes the root's row first, and a query on the base class joins every descendant's table to learn each row's concrete class. The documentation weighs the two: one table suits a simple, stable hierarchy queried across all its types, while a table per type keeps each table's constraints honest at the cost of joins. What it adds is the part a polymorphic model cannot do without: loading each row back as the class it was saved as.

Signal state and its reducers notice a change by a new reference, so a rich object that edits its own fields in place, as most examples of the pattern do, would leave the page showing the old value; making every method return a new object keeps the screen right but turns the model into pure functions written as classes.
limits.item2: A model with few rules costs more than it saves. To learn what an import does, a reader follows fromExport into Step.from, into each step's class and into the scene's admit, where the transaction script could be read top to bottom. The app's compositions have a handful of checks, mostly about shape, and the engine's interpreters table already gives each step kind its own function, so classes would move that code without adding a rule.
limits.item3: The guarantee holds only while nothing goes round the constructors. In TypeScript a class with private fields cannot be imitated by an object literal, but a cast can still pass a plain object off as one, and a test fixture or a migration of stored data that builds compositions that way makes objects that never passed their checks, which the rest of the code, having stopped checking, will trust.

intuition.text: An object refers to another by holding it; a row can only hold the other row's key. Saving turns each reference into the key of the row it points at, which is the easy half. Loading turns keys back into references, and that is where the care goes: two keys naming one row should become one object, and keys that lead back to where they started must not be followed for ever.
intuition.situation: The catalog's rows relate to one another by id: Data Mapper's row keeps the ids of Identity Map and Unit of Work, and both of theirs keep Data Mapper's. Anything that turns those ids into objects, a reading that showed each relation's own relations, say, or an export that wrote the whole graph, has to know when it has met a row before.

example.name: Opening Data Mapper's relations
example.description: Three PoEAA rows of the catalog relate to one another. Data Mapper, whose id is poeaa:{lineDataMapper}, keeps the keys of Identity Map, poeaa:{lineIdentityMap}, and of Unit of Work, poeaa:{lineUnitOfWork}, and each of those keeps the keys of the other two; of each row's relations the example keeps only these. A loader opens Data Mapper and turns every key it meets into a reference to an object, following each key to the end before taking the next. {resolving}

step0.title: Store each reference as a key
step0.text: Saving keeps only the key of each row an object refers to: Data Mapper's row holds poeaa:{lineIdentityMap} and poeaa:{lineUnitOfWork}, never the objects. Here the keys sit on the referring row as a list, because the row is read whole; a relational table cannot hold a list in a column, so a one-to-many collection puts its key on each row of the many side instead, pointing back at the parent.

step1.title: Read the row, register its object
step1.text: To load a row the loader reads it, builds its object and enters it in the identity map before following any key. Entering it first is what lets a key that leads back to it find it there. Objects built so far: {objects}.

step2.title: Follow the keys in order
step2.text: Each key in turn becomes a reference, and a key that loads a new row finishes that row's keys before the next key here is taken. A row is resolved when its last key is a reference, so Data Mapper, whose first key led round the whole cycle, finishes last.

step3.title: Resolve a key through the identity map
step3.text: A key whose row is already in the identity map becomes a reference to that very object, with no read; any other key loads its row. Rows read so far: {reads}, of {rows} rows; references made: {references}.

pseudocode.ordinary:
save(object):
  keys = [target.id for target in object.related]
  store.write({ id: object.id, keys: keys })

load(id):
  row = store.read(id)
  object = { id: id, related: [] }
  identityMap[id] = object
  follow(object, row.keys)
  return object

follow(object, keys):
  for key in keys:
    object.related.add(resolve(key))

resolve(key):
  if key in identityMap:
    return identityMap[key]
  return load(key)

item0.project: DotLn-Angular · join-maps and the reading's relation links
item0.relevance: This script joins the research run's maps into the catalog the app ships, and it is where a concept's relations, named by title in the maps, become the ids the reading links by.
item0.explanation: The author's reading of the code, not a claim that it was designed as this pattern: each mined relation is a title, and the join stores it on the referring row as that title with an id beside it, the id of the one other row in the same work with exactly that title, or null when there is none, when there are several, or when the title is the row's own. The key thus sits on the referrer's row, and check-catalog refuses one that names a missing row, a row of another work or the row itself. The reading never builds the target: it shows the stored title and turns the key into a link with hrefFor, and only when the reader follows it does CatalogStore look the row up among the loaded tools, ignoring an id it does not have. That is one key at a time and only on demand, so the cycle this study's loader meets never arises. Where it parts from the pattern: the related list is a collection kept on the referring side, many-to-many in nature, which a relational schema would give an association table; nothing lists what links to a concept; and every join rebuilds every list from the maps, the delete-and-reinsert way of updating a collection.

item1.project: Hibernate ORM · associations in the user guide
item1.relevance: Hibernate is a Java object-relational mapper and an implementation of Jakarta Persistence; the associations chapter of its user guide shows, beside each mapping, the tables it expects and the SQL it runs.
item1.explanation: A @ManyToOne field becomes a foreign key column on the child's own table: Hibernate sets it when the reference is set and updates it to NULL when the reference is cleared. A @OneToMany collection with no matching @ManyToOne is kept in a link table instead, and removing one child makes Hibernate delete every link row of that parent and insert again the ones still in the collection. Made bidirectional with mappedBy, the child side owns the single foreign key, and removing a child costs one update that sets that column to NULL.

item2.relevance: Spring Data JDBC is the Spring Data module for plain JDBC, built round aggregates; its mapping reference says where the key goes for each kind of reference, and which references it will not map as objects at all.
item2.explanation: Inside an aggregate every reference, whether to one entity or to a Set, List or Map of them, becomes a foreign key on the referenced entity's table pointing back at the referencing one, named by default after the referencing table, with an extra key column for a List's index or a Map's key. References are one-to-one or one-to-many only: a many-to-one or many-to-many relation means two aggregates, and between aggregates the reference is a plain id, best wrapped in an AggregateReference, which also records in its type which aggregate the id names.

item0.supports: The pattern's name and its short statement there: an association between objects is saved as a foreign key between tables, because a reference means something only inside the running program; the page also notes that a collection of references does not fit a relational table.

item1.supports: The book itself (Addison-Wesley, 2002), where Foreign Key Mapping belongs to chapter 12, Object-Relational Structural Patterns. This study names the chapter and quotes nothing from it.

limits.item0: Choose to read every key's row (0) and step on: Unit of Work's key to Identity Map reads that row again and builds a second object, whose key to Unit of Work does the same, so the loader goes round the cycle until something stops it; this model stops it at {readLimit} reads, while a real loader stops only when its call stack overflows. A loader that stopped short of that would still hold several Identity Map objects, and a change made through one would never reach the others.
limits.item1: With the identity map the loader is safe but greedy: opening one row builds every row its keys reach, and in the catalog Data Mapper's keys reach dozens of PoEAA rows within a few hops. Resolving a key only when it is used, through a Lazy Load or the way the app's reading keeps a title beside each key and looks the row up when the link is followed, reads one row for each step the reader takes.
limits.item2: A key held where the join does not reach can come to name the wrong row. The join rebuilds every key inside the catalog, so those never go stale; but a reader's history in browser storage, a saved composition's tool ids and a study's nearby list also name rows by id, and an id is its map's line number, so a regenerated map with a line inserted above would make them name a different concept. That is why the catalog rules keep line-based ids stable.
limits.item3: Saving new objects that refer to one another needs an order. A key can be written only once the row it names has an id and, where the store checks keys, exists, so a cycle of new objects with generated ids has to write one key empty and fill it in by a later update.

intuition.text: A gateway is where the app and an outside resource meet, and it translates in both directions. Going out, an intention in the app's words, load the board, becomes the resource's request: an address, a method, a time limit. Coming back, everything the resource can do, answer, refuse, stall or drop the connection, becomes one of the app's own shapes. Read a gateway by asking what it lets cross unchanged; the answer should be nothing.
intuition.situation: The board page reads the actor board from the app's HTTP API. Its store should not know the API's address, how long to wait, or what a 503 or a dropped connection looks like on the wire; it wants a board, or the reason it has none. When the API moves, slows down or is replaced by a stub for a test, only the gateway should have to change.

example.name: One board request, through the front and the back
example.description: The board store needs its document and calls the gateway's one method, load. The front names the board's route; the back sends the request to the app's HTTP API and waits at most {timeoutMs} ms. The API answers after {answerMs} ms with status {status} and a board of contract version {servedVersion}. The board page draws version {pageVersion}.

step0.title: Ask in the app's terms
step0.text: The store calls load() on the gateway's front, and that is all it knows of the API: no address, no time limit, no status codes. The front adds only which resource the app means, the path of the board's route, and hands the request to the back.

step1.title: Add what the transport needs
step1.text: The back resolves the path against the API's base address from configuration, sets a time limit of {timeoutMs} ms and sends the request. Neither the address nor the limit is visible above it.

step2.title: Wait, or stop waiting
step2.text: An answer inside the limit is received in the API's terms: a status and a body. When the limit passes first, the back abandons the request and raises the transport's own timeout; a connection lost before any answer is raised the same way.

step3.title: Translate on the way in
step3.text: The back turns what came back into the app's terms: a 2xx status into a board, any other status into an HTTP failure, a timeout or a lost connection into failures of those kinds. It checks nothing else, so the board's contract version crosses as it came. Terms of the API that have crossed untranslated: {untranslated}.

step4.title: Hand back one of two shapes
step4.text: The front returns the outcome in the app's own types, and the store records loadSuccess or loadFailure. The store holds {outcome}.

item0.project: DotLn-Angular · BoardApi with the HTTP interceptors
item0.relevance: This app's board reads its uifa-board-v1 document through BoardApi, a one-method class over Angular's HttpClient; the API's base address, the time limit and the mapping of errors live in the interceptors the app installs on every HTTP call.
item0.explanation: The author's reading of the code, not a claim that it was designed as this pattern: BoardApi.load() is the front, shaped to the board store's single need and typed with the app's BoardResponse. The interceptors installed by provideDotlnHttp behave as its back: baseUrlInterceptor resolves the path against the configured apiBaseUrl, timeoutInterceptor applies requestTimeoutMs, and errorInterceptor turns HTTP, network and timeout errors into the app's AppError and announces each one on the app's event stream. Where it stops: that back is shared by every HTTP call rather than owned by the board, so the board's translation cannot be read in one file; the response is typed, not checked, so BoardResponse admits any viewModelVersion string and the version check waits in BoardFacade, past the gateway; and the specs replace the API with MSW at the network instead of replacing the back.

item1.relevance: Angular's own HTTP client, which this app's gateway is built on, is split the same way inside: HttpClient is the interface application code calls, and HttpBackend is the last handler, the one that actually dispatches the request.
item1.explanation: HttpBackend is an abstract injectable class with one method, handle, which turns an HttpRequest into a stream of HttpEvents; by default it is the fetch-based backend. Interceptors sit between HttpClient and the backend, and HttpInterceptorHandler chains them in the order they were provided before handing the request on. Because the backend is a token like any other, a test can provide a different one: the source notes that once the testing backend is provided no HTTP calls are made at all, which is the front-and-back split doing exactly what it is for.

item2.relevance: JdbcTemplate is Spring's long-standing wrapper over JDBC, whose connections, statements and checked SQLExceptions are the kind of awkward API a gateway exists to keep out of application code.
item2.explanation: Callers supply the SQL and a callback such as a RowMapper; the template obtains and releases the connection, creates the statement and applies settings such as the fetch size and the query timeout. Every SQLException goes through a pluggable SQLExceptionTranslator into Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy, and one the translator cannot classify still crosses as an UncategorizedSQLException, so no caller ever handles the driver's own exception. Its documentation now points to JdbcClient, added in 6.1, as a more focused front that delegates to it.

item0.title: Gateway, in Martin Fowler's online catalog of the book's patterns
item0.supports: The pattern's name and its short statement: access to an outside system or resource is wrapped in one object, so the rest of the code calls ordinary methods and leaves the resource's specialised API to that object.

item1.title: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture, the publisher's page
item1.supports: The book itself (Addison-Wesley, 2002), where Gateway belongs to chapter 18, Base Patterns. This study names the chapter and quotes nothing from it.

limits.item0: A thin gateway translates only what it has a rule for. Set the served version to 2 and step to the delivery: the back translates status, time and connection but has no rule for the board's contract version, so a version-2 board crosses as a board, the store keeps it as its document, and nothing fails until the page tries to draw it. In this app that check sits in the board's facade, past the gateway, which is why an unsupported version first shows on the board page rather than in the store.
limits.item1: A translated timeout loses what the API did. Set the API's answer time past the limit: the back abandons the request at {timeoutMs} ms and raises its own timeout, so the store learns only that it waited too long, not whether the API finished the work. For the board, a read, that is harmless; behind a gateway that writes, a lost save and a slow one look the same, and retrying may apply it twice.
limits.item2: A gateway that starts deciding hides the resource instead of translating it. Retrying a refusal, falling back to a recorded board or caching the last document turns the gateway into a second store with rules of its own, and a stub then has to reproduce those rules before any test means anything. This app keeps the recorded board out of production for that reason: it is never a fallback.
limits.item3: The front is shaped to one caller. The board store needs one method that returns one document; a second caller that wants a single panel, or a write, either bends that method or adds its own, and after a few such additions the front mirrors the API it was meant to hide. One small gateway per need usually reads better than one that serves everyone.

item2.why: When the resource is a database table: one gateway object per table, with a method for each query, is this pattern specialised for relational data.

item3.why: When each row should have a gateway of its own: an object that holds one row's fields and knows how to insert and update itself.

intuition.text: A store tells rows apart by key; a running program tells objects apart by which object each one is. Identity Field is the bridge: the object carries its row's key, so code holding the object can reach the right row, and code holding only the key can find the object again. Storing the key is the easy part; the real work is in choosing it, because a key has to be unique and has to stay the same for good, and both promises depend on who hands keys out and what that chooser can see.
intuition.situation: The soldier scene saves compositions to browser storage, each under an id such as composition-3, and the saved list opens a composition by that id. When two tabs are open on the scene and both save, each new composition needs a key that no other composition, in either tab, holds or will hold.

example.name: Two tabs, one numbering
example.description: Browser storage holds two compositions, Flank left as composition-{keyFlank} and Hold the ridge as composition-{keyRidge}, and two tabs have read that list. The operator composes Dawn raid in the other tab and Night march in this one; the other tab saves first, then this tab, and each tab then opens the key Dawn raid was given. A new key is one past the highest number in the list the save reads. {rereadSentence}

step0.title: Read each object with its key
step0.text: Loading the stored list gives every composition its key along with its title and steps. The key is a field of the object itself, not a value looked up beside it.

step1.title: Leave a new object without one
step1.text: A composition just made has no key yet. It cannot be opened from the saved list, and nothing should refer to it by key until a save gives it one.

step2.title: Choose the next key from the freshest list
step2.text: The key is one past the highest number in the list the save reads. That is safe only if the list holds every key already given out, which is why the scene's save reads storage again just before choosing.

step3.title: Store the key in the object, then write
step3.text: The key is set on the composition before the list is written, so the object and its stored copy carry the same key from then on. Keys held by two compositions at this step: {collisions}.

step4.title: Find by key
step4.text: Opening a composition takes the first in the list with that key. With unique keys that is the same composition wherever the key is opened; once a key is shared, what it opens depends on which list is asked, and within one list whichever comes second cannot be opened by it at all.

pseudocode.ordinary:
load():
  list = storage.read()
  every composition in list keeps its own id

compose(title, steps):
  return { id: none, title, steps }

save(composition):
  list = storage.read()
  highest = largest number ending an id in list, or 0
  key = 'composition-' + (highest + 1)

  composition.id = key
  list.append(composition)
  storage.write(list)

open(key):
  return the first composition in list whose id is key

item0.relevance: SceneFacade runs the soldier scene and saves the operator's compositions to browser storage through SceneStore, each under an id it chooses itself.
item0.explanation: The author's reading of the code, not a claim that it was designed as this pattern: every Composition carries its id as a field, a meaningless key of the form composition-N, and open(id) uses it to find the composition in the saved list. nextCompositionId takes one past the highest trailing number in the list rather than its length, because the list may have gaps where a stored composition could not be read. save() reads storage again before choosing, since another tab may have saved in the meantime, and skips that re-read after a failed save so as not to lose the only copy of the unsaved composition, so the next key then comes from the list this tab holds. The key is unique only within the one stored list, and only by that care: restoreStoredScene checks that an id is a non-empty string, not that no other composition has it, and open(id) takes the first match. An imported composition is opened as a run rather than added to the list, so its saved copy gets a fresh key.

item1.relevance: Jakarta Persistence, formerly JPA, is the standard Java persistence API that Hibernate implements, and GenerationType names the strategies a provider may use to generate an entity's primary key.
item1.explanation: Its five constants read as the pattern's key-generation choices turned into an API: TABLE keeps a database table that hands out unique keys, a key table; SEQUENCE draws from a database sequence; IDENTITY lets an identity column assign the key at insert; UUID generates an RFC 4122 universally unique identifier, held as a UUID or a String; and AUTO leaves the choice to the provider, which takes UUID for those key types and one of the three numeric strategies for integer keys. None of them asks the application to scan for the highest key, the step that needs every key in view.

item2.relevance: TypeORM is a TypeScript object-relational mapper, and this decorator marks the property of an entity that holds its generated primary key.
item2.explanation: The decorator takes a strategy, increment by default, or uuid, rowid or identity. When no column type is given it chooses one from the strategy, a number for increment and identity and a uuid column for uuid, then marks the column as primary and records the strategy as generation metadata for the rest of the mapper to act on, so the entity class states once how its key is made.

item0.title: Identity Field, in Martin Fowler's online catalog of the book's patterns
item0.supports: The pattern's name and its short statement: an object keeps its database row's key in one of its fields so that it stays tied to that row, because the database tells rows apart by key while the language tells objects apart by themselves.

item1.title: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture, the publisher's page
item1.supports: The book itself (Addison-Wesley, 2002), where Identity Field belongs to chapter 12, Object-Relational Structural Patterns. This study names the chapter and quotes nothing from it.

limits.item0: A key chosen as one past the highest is unique only if the chooser sees every key already given. Set the re-reads to 0 and step to the second save: this tab chooses from the list it read at the start and takes the key the other tab gave Dawn raid a moment before, so one key now names two compositions. Because a save writes the whole list, storage keeps Night march under that key and drops Dawn raid, which survives only in the other tab's memory until that tab reads storage again. The scene's save accepts this risk on purpose after a failed save, to keep the one copy of an unsaved composition.
limits.item1: Highest-plus-one also hands a number out again once the highest is gone. The scene cannot delete a saved composition yet; once it can, deleting the newest gives its number to the next save, and any reference kept under the old key would open a different composition. A counter kept apart from the list, as a key table keeps it, or a random UUID never reuses a key.
limits.item2: A meaningful key is only as stable as its meaning. The catalog's own ids are the other kind: poeaa:268 is line 268 of the PoEAA map, so a row inserted above it in a new mining run would leave every key below it naming a different concept. The catalog join guards that by refusing a map whose bytes no longer match their recorded SHA-256 digest, which freezes the meaning rather than making the key meaningless.
limits.item3: Not every object needs a key. A composition's steps carry none: they are only ever read, written and found through the composition that holds them, so a key of their own would identify nothing anyone looks up.

intuition.text: An identity map makes two kinds of identity agree for as long as a session lasts: the store's, where an id names one row, and the language's, where === says two references are one object. Ask twice for the same id and the same object comes back, so the second ask costs no read and nothing on the page can hold an older or a newer copy. Most of what goes wrong with the pattern happens at its two edges: which callers share the map, and when it is thrown away.
intuition.situation: A study's reading and the list of nearby concepts beside it both look concepts up by id. When Identity Map's nearby list names Unit of Work, which the reader opened a moment ago, the list should be handed the object the reading already holds, not fetch a second one that may already say something different about the same study.

example.name: Two callers, one map
example.description: Suppose the catalog's mining API serves each study by its concept id, as the CatalogLoader interface allows, through a loader that keeps an identity map for the session. The reader opens Unit of Work (poeaa:246); the reviewers' check of that study then lands in the store; the reader follows a link to Identity Map (poeaa:254), whose nearby list asks for Unit of Work; the reader {revisitsPhrase}, then reloads the page and opens Unit of Work once more. {mapsSentence}

step0.title: Ask the map first
step0.text: Every lookup starts at the map, under the concept's id. A hit hands back the object already held: no read, and every caller that asked holds that same object. Hits so far: {hits}.

step1.title: Read on a miss, then keep the result
step1.text: Only an id the map lacks reaches the store. The loader builds the object from that one read and keeps it under the id before returning it, so the next lookup of the id is a hit. Store reads so far: {reads}; lookups: {lookups}.

step2.title: Share one map across the session
step2.text: A map protects only the callers that ask it. Every path that can reach a study has to go through the same loader; a second loader starts a second map, and one row becomes two objects that need not agree.

step3.title: Throw it away when the session ends
step3.text: The map answers with what it read, so a change saved to the store during the session stays unseen until the map is discarded. A new session starts empty and reads each study afresh.

pseudocode.ordinary:
find(id):
  if map.has(id):
    return map.get(id)

  row = store.read(id)
  study = studyFrom(row)
  map.set(id, study)
  return study

provideCatalog():
  loader = { map: new Map(), find }
  reading.loader = loader
  nearbyList.loader = loader

endSession():
  loader.map = new Map()

item0.explanation: The author's reading of the code, not a claim that it was designed as this pattern: its cached helper keeps one pending or settled promise per key and forgets a failed one so that a retry can run, and loadWork does the same for a work's tool chunks, so two callers asking for the same work share one load and receive the same objects. Three things separate it from the pattern. The key is a work, not a concept: study(id) finds the concept by scanning the cached chunk on every call. Nothing is ever cleared, so the map lasts as long as its loader. And the map belongs to a loader, not to the app: CatalogToken has no root provider, and the Tools routes and the soldier scene each call provideCatalog() in their own route providers, so each keeps a cache of its own. item1.relevance: MikroORM is a TypeScript object-relational mapper for Node.js, and this internal class holds its managed entities, one instance per row.
item1.explanation: It keeps one inner Map per entity class inside a registry Map, so it is the map-per-class form behind a single front, with each entity stored under a hash of its primary key. It can also index an entity under the values of other unique properties, its target keys, so that a reference made through such a key finds the same instance, and delete removes those extra entries only where they still point at the deleted entity, since swapping unique values can hand one to another entity. clear empties every class's map at once.

item2.relevance: Hibernate is a widely used Jakarta Persistence provider for Java, and its persistence context, one for each session, is where its identity map lives.
item2.explanation: Loaded entities of every class share one HashMap, keyed by EntityKey, which carries the entity's persister as well as its identifier, so the single map still tells two classes' rows apart. getEntity answers null both for a key it lacks and for a holder whose entity is not yet initialised, and addEntityHolder uses putIfAbsent, so registering an entity under a key that already has a holder fills that holder rather than starting a second. A separate map indexes entities by other unique keys, and clear empties the context.

limits.item0: Within a session the map is a snapshot. Step to the hit after the store changes: Unit of Work is checked in the store, yet every lookup still returns the draft read before the check, and only the new session sees the change. A long-lived session needs an explicit refresh, a re-read into the object the map already holds, or a shorter scope.
limits.item1: The map promises one object only to the callers that share it. Set the maps to 2: the nearby list misses in its own map, reads Unit of Work again and shows it checked while the reading beside it still shows the draft, at the cost of another read. limits.item3: The map keeps every object it has handed out until the session ends; that is the price of the promise. intuition.text: Laziness does not remove a cost; it moves the cost to the moment someone needs the data, and lets it vanish when nobody does. In this app the catalog keeps a short entry for each study, enough to say that a concept has one, and fetches the record only when a reading asks for it. The design question is how much one fetch brings back: one record, and a reader moving down a list pays a trip per item; a whole work, and the first reading fills memory with records nobody opens.
intuition.situation: The Tools catalog serves the concepts of six works, and a study record, with its prose keys, parameters, implementations and references, is far larger than the line that marks a concept as studied. Someone who opens two readings should not wait for every study the app has, nor download a study again on coming back to it.

example.name: Three readings, one chunk
example.description: The catalog has read the studies summary and holds no study record. The reader filters the catalog to studied concepts, then opens the readings of Lazy Load, Unit of Work and Record Set, in that order. {chunking} {failure}

step0.title: Keep a marker
step0.text: The studies summary names each study by id and state and holds nothing else. That entry is the marker: the catalog marks, counts and filters studied concepts from it with no record in memory.

step1.title: Fetch on the first read
step1.text: The first read of a study looks up its work in the summary and asks for that work's chunk, keeping the pending load under the work's name. A concept with no study answers none and loads nothing. Chunk requests so far: {requests}.

step2.title: Bring the collection at once
step2.text: The chunk carries every study of the work, so one request fills them all, however few the reader opens. Splitting it per study would cost a request for every study read instead. Records in memory now: {records}.

step3.title: Answer later reads from what was kept
step3.text: A later read of any study of the work finds the kept load and waits on it, so it costs no request, and every reading receives the same record.

step4.title: Forget a failed load
step4.text: When the import fails, the kept load is dropped, the records are markers again and the reading offers a retry, so the next read asks once more. A loader that kept the failure would refuse every later read of the work without trying.

pseudocode.ordinary:
markers = readSummary()               # each study's id and state, no record
isStudied(id): return markers.has(id)

study(id):
  work = markers.workOf(id)
  if work is none: return none        # a concept with no study loads nothing
  return (await chunk(work)).find(id)

chunk(work):
  if work not in kept:
    kept[work] = import(chunkFile(work))   # every study of the work, one request

  return kept[work]                   # a later read waits on the same load

on kept[work] failing:
  delete kept[work]                   # a marker again: the next read asks anew
  report the failure to the reading

item1.relevance: TypeORM is a TypeScript object-relational mapper. A relation whose property is typed as a Promise loads lazily, which puts the Value Holder form in the language this app is written in.
item1.explanation: enableLazyLoad replaces the relation's property on each entity with a getter. The first read starts the relation's query and keeps its pending promise on the entity; a read while it is pending returns that same promise; once it resolves, the data is stored and later reads resolve from it without a query. item2.explanation: The guide separates when data is fetched, eagerly or lazily, from how: a separate select, a join, a batch or a subselect. A lazy association loaded by separate selects is the strategy it says is generally called N+1, one query for each object reached. Its @BatchSize answer works on uninitialised entity proxies: once several departments are loaded, their employees arrive through one IN-restricted select, two statements in the guide's example where separate selects would need ten. intuition.text: An optimistic lock is a bet that two people seldom change the same thing at the same moment. Nothing is held while anyone works, so opening and editing cost nothing and never wait. The bet is settled when someone saves: a version number shows whether the record moved underneath, and if it did, whoever saves second pays for the collision with the work done since they opened it.
intuition.situation: In this example the operator has Hold the ridge open in two browser tabs, trying a different change in each, and a save replaces the stored copy. Both tabs read the same version. If both save, the second must not silently erase the first: under an optimistic lock it is refused, and that tab is told the composition changed while it worked.

example.name: Two tabs, one composition
example.description: Hold the ridge is in browser storage at version {version}. Tab A opens it and works on it for {minutesA} minutes; {openB} minutes later Tab B opens it too and works for {minutesB} minutes. {ending} Neither tab takes a lock: each remembers the version it read, and a save writes only if storage still holds that version. A refused tab reloads and does its work again.

step0.title: Read and remember
step0.text: Opening the composition reads it with its version, and the tab keeps that number. Nothing is written and nothing is held, so any number of tabs may open it at once.

step1.title: Change in the tab only
step1.text: Edits change the tab's own copy. Storage does not know the tab is editing, and the other tab is never slowed or warned.

step2.title: Save on condition
step2.text: A save writes only where storage still holds the version the tab read, and moves the version on by one. The check and the write have to be one step, or another tab's save can land between them. Storage holds version {stored} now.

step3.title: Refuse a stale save
step3.text: If the version has moved, nothing is written: the tab's changes are refused and the operator is told another tab saved first. Saves refused so far: {refusals}; minutes of work thrown away: {lost}.

step4.title: Reload and redo
step4.text: The refused tab reads the composition again at its new version and makes its changes again, or merges them, then saves. That save succeeds unless another one beats it.

pseudocode.ordinary:
open(tab):
  row = storage.read("Hold the ridge")
  tab.copy = row.composition
  tab.version = row.version

edit(tab, change):
  tab.copy = change(tab.copy)

save(tab):
  written = storage.writeIf(version == tab.version,
                            "Hold the ridge", tab.copy,
                            version: tab.version + 1)
  if not written: return refuse(tab)
  tab.version = tab.version + 1

refuse(tab):
  refusals = refusals + 1
  tell the operator: Hold the ridge changed in another tab
  discard tab.copy

reload(tab):
  open(tab)
  redo or merge the refused changes
  save(tab)

item0.explanation: The author's reading of the code, not a claim that it was designed as this pattern. Before saving, save re-reads the stored list through withPersistedState's readFromStorage, unless the last save failed, because, as its comment says, another tab may have saved since this one read the list, and a save writes the whole list. It then appends the new composition under the next free id, and withPersistedState writes the list back with setItem. The re-read is the first half of an optimistic check, a look at what storage holds at the moment of saving, but nothing is compared and nothing is refused. That is enough only because a save never changes a stored composition: it adds one, so two tabs that open the same composition and both save end with two new ones and lose neither. The stored value's version: 1 names its shape, not a revision, and the writeOn counter counts this tab's own saves. If a save replaced the composition it opened, the re-read would bring in the other tab's save and this one would overwrite it without a word; the check would sit between the re-read and the dispatch, comparing a revision noted when the composition was opened with the one just read. A cousin already runs in ToolsFacade, whose study load remembers the sequence number it started with and drops its answer when a later load has moved the number on.

item1.relevance: Active Record is the object-relational mapper of Ruby on Rails, and this module is the pattern under its own name, switched on by a lock_version column.
item1.explanation: Every update adds a version to its conditions, the one the object was loaded with or, when the application has assigned lock_version, the value it assigned, and increments the column; when the update touches anything other than one row it raises StaleObjectError and puts the in-memory version back, and a destroy is checked the same way. Its documentation notes that this works within one Ruby process and that, across web requests, the version should travel with the form as a hidden field; that assigned value is what the condition then checks, which is the offline part: the version the operator's page read comes back with the save. What to do on a conflict, roll back, merge or ask, is left to the application.

item2.relevance: MikroORM is a TypeScript object-relational mapper; once an entity declares a version property, its unit of work makes this check on every update it commits.
item2.explanation: The persister adds the entity's version to each update's where condition and throws OptimisticLockError when no row is affected. Before a batch of updates it first looks every row up by key and version and refuses if any is missing, then refuses again if the batch wrote fewer rows than it sent. An entity without a version column can name concurrency-check properties instead, whose original values join the condition. For the offline case, em.lock with LockMode.OPTIMISTIC and the version a client sent back compares that version with the loaded one and refuses before any change is made.

limits.item0: An optimistic lock is the wrong choice when collisions are likely and the work is long. Tab B here loses everything it did after opening the composition; raise the minutes Tab B works and the loss rises with them, and redoing the work takes as long again. Two tabs left open on one composition all afternoon are a likely collision, and the pessimistic lock, which turns Tab B away when it opens, costs a wait instead. Nor does opening first protect a tab: lower Tab B's minutes until it saves first, and Tab A, which opened earlier, is the one refused.
limits.item1: Browser storage has no conditional write. Reading the stored version and calling setItem are two calls, and nothing stops another tab's write landing between them, so a check written that way narrows the gap without closing it. Closing it needs both calls under one lock, such as the browser's Web Locks API, or a server that updates only where the version still matches.
limits.item2: The check covers only what the save writes. If Tab B's change depends on something it merely read, such as steps copied from another composition, a rival save of that one passes unnoticed unless the save checks its version too, and the stored result is then right record by record and wrong as a whole.
limits.item3: One version for the whole stored list would refuse too much. The app keeps every composition under one storage key, so the version simplest to keep is one for the key, and then a save of Hold the ridge is refused because the other tab saved a different composition. A version per composition avoids those false conflicts, at the cost of merging the list on every save.
limits.item4: A refusal detects the conflict and resolves nothing. The refused tab still holds its own steps, so it could show both versions and let the operator merge them instead of throwing the work away, but the lock gives no help with that merge; it only says one is needed.

intuition.text: Give every page of an application a small handler of its own. When a request for that page arrives, its handler reads what the request carries, asks the rest of the application for what the page needs, and picks how the answer is shown. Only the routing that finds the handler is shared, so each page can be read and changed on its own, at the price of every page repeating whatever all pages have to do.
intuition.situation: A reader pastes the link to a reading into a new tab. Whatever the address says, one piece of code decides what it means for the catalog page — open that reading, go back to the one before, or say the catalog has no such concept — and which of the page's views to show. A colleague asking where a reading's address is handled has one file to open.

example.name: Opening a reading from its address
example.description: A reader follows a link to a reading, an address made of /tools/catalog/ and the concept's id, such as this page's own. The router matches the address to its route and hands the id to the catalog page, the controller for that one logical page. The page works out what the address means against what it already shows, tells the catalog store, and picks a view from the store's answer: the reading, a notice that the address names nothing, a loading line, or a failure with a retry. The Tools home, at /tools, has a controller of its own that does the same three things for its page.

step0.title: One route, one controller
step0.text: The route table gives each logical page its own controller: the Tools home one, and the catalog and a single reading the catalog page. A reading's address carries the concept's id as a parameter of its route, and the router binds it to the page's input.

step1.title: Decode the request
step1.text: The catalog page reads the id from the address and works out what it means against what the page already shows: nothing new, a new reading, the reading it came from, or an id the catalog does not have.

step2.title: Invoke the model
step2.text: It hands one event to the catalog store, which owns the readings, the history and the back stack, and puts away the study state of the reading it left. The page decides what the address means; the store decides what opening a reading changes.

step3.title: Choose the view
step3.text: From the store's answer the page picks one of its views: a loading line, a failure with a retry, the reading, a notice that the address names nothing, or the invitation to choose a concept.

step4.title: Every page repeats the frame
step4.text: The Tools home's controller does the same three things for its own page: it says that it opened, the store loads the summary for it, and it picks between its shelf and a failure with a retry.

pseudocode.ordinary:
routes:
  /tools                 -> ToolsHomePage
  /tools/catalog         -> CatalogPage
  /tools/catalog/:toolId -> CatalogPage

CatalogPage.arrive(address):
  id = address.toolId
  if id == shown: return unchanged
  if id not in catalog: event = readingClosed
  else if id == backStack.last: event = readingReturned
  else: event = conceptOpened(id)

  store.dispatch(event)
  leaveStudy()

  view = store.loading ? loadingLine
       : store.failed ? failureWithRetry
       : store.selected ? reading(store.selected)
       : id ? unknownReadingNotice
       : invitation
  render(view)

ToolsHomePage.open():
  store.dispatch(toolsHome.opened)
  view = store.summaryFailed ? failureWithRetry : shelf(store.summary)
  render(view)

item0.relevance: The catalog page is the routed container that answers both the catalog's address and every reading's address; with the facade it provides for itself, it is the app's clearest controller for one logical page.
item0.explanation: The author's reading of the code, not a claim that it was designed as this pattern. The Tools routes give the Tools home and the catalog page a container each, and the catalog page lists ToolsFacade among its own providers, so its controller lives and dies with the page. The router binds the address's toolId to the page's input; an effect hands it to facade.arrive, which decides whether the address opens a reading, returns to the previous one or closes it, and dispatches that event to the catalog store the Tools routes share. The page's template then picks a view: loading, failure with a retry, the reading, an unknown reading, or the invitation. It stops being a page controller in the classic sense in three ways. No server request reaches it: Angular's router is the single entry that matches every address and creates the page, which is the dispatching half of a front controller. One controller answers two addresses. And moving from one reading to another keeps the same page, because the router reuses a component whose route has not changed, so the controller sees a changed input, not a new request, and arrive has to work out what changed.

item1.relevance: eShopOnWeb, Microsoft's reference ASP.NET Core application, builds its web pages with Razor Pages, where each page is a template with a code-behind PageModel class; the basket page's model is a page controller in that shape.

item0.supports: The pattern's name and a short statement of it, here in the author's words: a handler for each page or action of a site, which may be the page itself or a separate object.

limits.item0: Shared steps are copied page by page. The Tools home and the catalog page each dispatch their own opened event and each draw their own failure with a retry, and they meet the catalog differently: the catalog page waits for it to load before reading the address, while the Tools home shows its shelf from the summary alone. A third page would copy those steps again; a step every page must take first is better run once, by a front controller.
limits.item1: In a browser a page controller is not called once per request. Moving between readings keeps the same catalog page, so its controller sees only a changed id; code written as if each request started fresh, such as moving the focus to the reading only when the page is created, misses every move after the first.
limits.item2: Rules collect in the controller because it is the easy place to put them. Deciding that an address equal to the top of the back stack means going back is a rule about reading history, yet it sits in the page's facade, not in the store that owns the history, and a second page that opened readings would need its own copy.
limits.item3: It says nothing about the flow between pages. Which page follows which — the scene link from a reading, the move back to the catalog when a work is chosen — is spread over each page's links and navigations; once that flow has rules of its own, it belongs in one application controller rather than in every page.

intuition.text: A pessimistic lock expects the collision and prevents it at the door. Before a tab may change the composition it must hold the lock, and only one tab can; any other is turned away at once and told who has it. Nobody loses work at the save, but everyone else waits, and the lock itself has to be looked after: handed out, released, and taken back from a tab that never returns.
intuition.situation: In this example the operator has Hold the ridge open in two browser tabs, and a save replaces the stored copy. When the second tab opens it, it learns at once that the first is editing, before it has changed anything, rather than finding out when it saves. The price shows when the first tab is closed without saving: its lock keeps the second tab out until the lock runs out.

example.name: Two tabs, one composition
example.description: Hold the ridge is in browser storage at version {version}. Tab A opens it and works on it for {minutesA} minutes; {openB} minutes later Tab B opens it too, to work for {minutesB} minutes once it holds the lock. {ending} Opening asks for the composition's exclusive lock, owned by the tab that opened it and lasting {timeout} minutes from when it was taken; after that, a waiting tab may take it over. A tab turned away asks again as soon as the lock is released or runs out.

step0.title: Lock before reading
step0.text: Opening the composition first asks the lock manager for its exclusive lock, keyed by the composition and owned by the tab. Only with the lock does the tab read Hold the ridge and start work.

step1.title: Turn away at the door
step1.text: A tab that finds the lock held is turned away at once and told which tab holds it, before it has changed anything; it waits and asks again. Minutes spent waiting so far: {waited}.

step2.title: Save and release
step2.text: A save first checks that the tab still owns the lock, then writes the composition and releases the lock in one step, so a waiting tab can take it and read the version just written, {stored} now.

step3.title: Let abandoned locks run out
step3.text: A lock lasts {timeout} minutes from when it was taken. Past that, a waiting tab may take it over, so a tab that has been closed cannot keep the others out for ever. The lock now: {lock}.

step4.title: Refuse a save without the lock
step4.text: A tab whose lock was taken over may no longer save: its changes are refused, exactly as an optimistic lock would refuse them. Minutes of work thrown away so far: {lost}.

pseudocode.ordinary:
open(tab):
  if not acquire("Hold the ridge", owner: tab):
    return wait(tab)
  tab.copy = storage.read("Hold the ridge")

wait(tab):
  tell the operator which tab holds the lock
  when the lock is released or runs out:
    open(tab)

save(tab):
  if locks["Hold the ridge"].owner != tab:
    return refuse(tab)
  storage.write("Hold the ridge", tab.copy)
  delete locks["Hold the ridge"]

acquire(key, owner):
  lock = locks[key]
  if lock and lock.owner != owner and now < lock.expires:
    return false
  locks[key] = { owner, expires: now + timeout }
  return true

refuse(tab):
  tell the operator the lock was taken over
  discard tab.copy

item0.project: DotLn-Angular · SceneFacade.open, where a lock would go
item0.relevance: This app's soldier scene opens a saved composition through SceneFacade.open, the path on which a pessimistic lock would have to be taken before a tab starts changing it.
item0.explanation: The author's reading of the code: the app takes no lock anywhere. open finds the composition in SceneStore's list, and #open replays it from its own seed and dispatches compositionOpened; nothing asks whether another tab has it open, and nothing in SceneStore or browser storage records who does. A pessimistic lock would be taken at the start of #open, the one path that open and importJson share, keyed by the composition's id and owned by the tab, and released in save and in clear, which puts the composition down; a refusal would stop #open before the replay and tell the operator which tab has it. The lock itself would need a home: a second browser storage key holding each lock's owner and expiry, or the browser's Web Locks API, which lets only one script in an origin hold a named lock at a time. None of it is needed today, because a save adds a new composition rather than changing the one opened.

item1.relevance: WordPress is a PHP publishing system, and its post editor keeps two people from editing one post at once with a lock stored beside the post.
item1.explanation: wp_set_post_lock writes the lock as post metadata under _edit_lock, the current time and the user's id, and wp_check_post_lock returns the other user who holds it while it is younger than a window of 150 seconds, which a filter can change; an older lock counts as none, so a lock nobody sets again lapses by itself. The notice that follows them in the same file tells the second user who is editing and, unless a filter forbids it, offers to take over. The lock belongs to a user, not a browser tab: the check ignores a lock the current user holds, so one person's two tabs are not kept apart.

item2.relevance: Spring Integration's JDBC lock registry hands out locks shared by every instance of an application, and this repository is its lock table: a lock manager of the kind the pattern needs, kept in the database.
item2.explanation: Each lock is a row of the LOCK table, keyed by region and lock key, naming its owner, the repository's own client id, and when it expires. acquire first updates the row where it is already the owner's or has expired, and otherwise inserts one; if another owner's live row is there the insert breaks the key, and acquire answers false at once instead of waiting. delete releases a lock only for its owner, renew pushes its expiry on, and deleteExpired clears the abandoned ones. The registry offers these locks to code running in several application instances rather than to people at screens, but the table is the same: a key, an owner and a timeout.

item0.title: Pessimistic Offline Lock, in Martin Fowler's online catalog of the book's patterns
item0.supports: That the pattern is David Rice's; that it lets one business transaction at a time use the data by making it take a lock before it starts; and that it answers the late failures of an optimistic lock, where several sessions do their work and all but one learn only at the end that it was wasted.

item1.title: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture, the publisher's page
item1.supports: The book itself (Addison-Wesley, 2002), where Pessimistic Offline Lock, by David Rice, follows Optimistic Offline Lock in chapter 16, Offline Concurrency Patterns, with a simple lock manager as its worked example. This study names the chapter and quotes nothing from it.

limits.item0: An abandoned lock keeps everyone out until it runs out. Set the saves by Tab A to 0: its tab is closed with the lock still taken, and Tab B, which only wants to start, waits for the timeout rather than for anyone's work. In the same case an optimistic lock lets Tab B save the moment it is done, so a pessimistic lock is the wrong choice where collisions are rare and tabs are often left open.
limits.item1: A timeout shorter than the work takes the lock from a tab still using it. Lower the lock's minutes below Tab A's working time: Tab B takes the lock over while Tab A is still at work, and Tab A's save is refused, the very loss the lock was meant to prevent. Renewing the lock while a tab works, as Spring Integration's renew allows, avoids this, but every open tab then has to keep renewing.
limits.item2: Who owns the lock decides what it protects. Keyed by the operator, as WordPress keys its post lock by user, it would not keep this example's tabs apart at all, since both belong to the one person; here each tab has to be an owner of its own, which means giving every tab its own id.
limits.item3: Taking the lock must itself be safe between tabs. A lock table kept in browser storage is read and written in two calls, so two tabs opening at the same instant could both find it free and both believe they hold it. The browser's Web Locks API grants one holder at a time across an origin's tabs and can refuse at once instead of queueing, but it holds a lock only while a task in that tab is still running.

item0.why: Read it beside this one: the same two tabs with nothing taken at opening, so Tab B loses its work at the save instead of waiting at the door. Go there when collisions are rare or tabs are often left open.

item1.why: Locking Hold the ridge alone does not stop another tab saving a different composition into the same stored list; go there for locking the list, or a composition with its trials, as one.

item2.why: One way of opening that forgets the lock undoes it for every other, and importJson reaches #open as well as open does; go there for putting lock handling where every path passes.

item3.why: A save that needs two locks, say for two compositions merged into one, can leave two tabs each holding one and waiting for the other; go there for ordering locks or letting them time out.

intuition.text: Plugin moves one decision, which class stands behind an interface, out of code and into data. The code can then no longer get that decision wrong, and can no longer check it either: the compiler sees every implementation the build links, but not which one an environment will name. What the pattern buys is that an environment's choice changes without a build; what it costs is that a wrong choice is found only when that environment starts or, when the wrong choice is a valid one, not at all.
intuition.situation: The soldier scene paints every frame through one interface. In the browser that should be the canvas; in a unit test it should be a painter that draws nothing and lets the spec count what it was asked to draw. With the choice in each environment's configuration, no line of the scene tests which environment it is in.

example.name: A painter for each environment
example.description: The soldier scene draws through the SceneRenderer interface. The build links two painters under their names: canvas, which paints the 2D canvas, and null, which draws nothing and remembers what it was given. Each environment's configuration names one, and a plugin factory binds it at start-up: development names canvas and the unit tests name null. {productionConfig} The app binds its painter in code today, in provideSceneFeature and the scene test kit; the example moves that choice into configuration, which is the step Plugin adds.

step0.title: Link implementations under names
step0.text: The build links every painter that implements the interface under a short name, here canvas and null. Which painters exist is the only thing the code decides.

step1.title: Read the environment's configuration
step1.text: When an environment starts, the factory reads the painter its configuration names; production's configuration names {productionPainter}.

step2.title: Bind by name, or refuse
step2.text: The factory looks the name up among the linked painters and builds that one. A name the build does not link is refused there, at start-up, the first moment anything can notice it.

step3.title: Draw through the interface
step3.text: The scene calls draw on whatever was bound and never asks which painter it is. The canvas painter shows the frame and the null painter only counts it. Frames drawn so far: {drawn}; shown on a screen: {shown}.

pseudocode.ordinary:
linked = { canvas: CanvasPainter, null: NullPainter }

start(environment):
  name = readConfiguration(environment).painter
  bind(name)

bind(name):
  if name not in linked: refuse to start
  painter = new linked[name]()

drawFrame(frame):
  painter.draw(frame)
