item0.explanation: The author's reading of the code, not a claim that it was designed as this pattern: SceneRenderer, in renderers/scene-renderer.ts, is a separated interface whose comment says a later painter can implement it without the engine or the feature changing, and three classes implement it: CanvasSceneRenderer, NullSceneRenderer and TextSceneRenderer. SceneCanvas never names one; it injects SceneRendererFactoryToken and calls the factory it is given. provideSceneFeature binds that token to createCanvasRenderer, which itself returns the null painter where the browser gives no 2D context, and the scene test kit binds a factory returning one NullSceneRenderer whose draw count specs read. The seam and the choice per environment are there; what Plugin adds and the app lacks is configuration: both bindings are TypeScript in a providers list, compiled with the code, so changing production's painter takes a new build. TextSceneRenderer, which renders each frame as the text rows of the accessibility surface, is constructed directly by SceneFacade and is not swappable at all.

item1.relevance: Active Job is Rails' common interface for background jobs; which queueing backend runs them is named in each environment's configuration, so it is Plugin in everyday use.
item1.explanation: queue_adapter= accepts a name such as :sidekiq, turns it into a class with QueueAdapters.lookup, which fetches the constant named by the camelised name plus Adapter, and instantiates it; an object passed directly is accepted only if it answers enqueue and enqueue_at, the interface every adapter shares. Active Job's railtie supplies the default by environment, :test in the test environment and :async otherwise, and the test adapter stores enqueued jobs for assertions instead of running them, so a test suite gets a stub without any job class changing. Because the name is looked up as a constant, one with no adapter class behind it raises an error when the setting is applied.

item2.relevance: Spring's general-purpose mechanism, meant for use inside the framework, for finding the implementations of an extension interface that the JARs on the classpath declare, without any code naming them.
item2.explanation: Each JAR may carry a META-INF/spring.factories properties file whose keys are interface names and whose values list implementation class names. load(type) gathers the names for that interface from every such file, loads each class by name, checks that it is assignable to the interface, instantiates it through its single resolvable constructor and sorts the results by their declared order. By default a class it cannot load or instantiate becomes an IllegalArgumentException; a logging failure handler skips it instead. It returns every implementation listed rather than one, so an environment chooses by which JARs it puts on the classpath.

intuition.text: A table can leave the database and still behave like a table. Read the rows once, close the connection, and keep them in memory with their column names, holding beside every changed value the one that was read. A screen can draw the result without knowing what it holds, logic can work on it by column name, and when the work is done an adapter sends back only the rows that changed, each one guarded by the values it started from.
intuition.situation: The actor board already receives its projection as a table of this kind, and only reads it. The soldier scene's saved compositions are another table, and one the operator changes: shaped as a record set, a session could edit several of them away from the store and write them back in one pass, provided it knows what that pass does when one of those rows has changed somewhere else in the meantime.

example.name: Four changes written back row by row
example.description: Three compositions are stored: Screen the wood, Hold the bridge and Cross the ford. The session fills a record set with their title and note columns, edits the note of Screen the wood, renames Hold the bridge, deletes Cross the ford and adds Dawn raid, then hands the record set to an adapter that writes the changed rows back one at a time, in table order. {rival} {onError}

step0.title: Fill, then let go of the store
step0.text: One query fills the record set with its columns by name and its rows, each Unchanged and keeping the values it was read with as its originals. Nothing needs the store again until the write-back.

step1.title: Change a cell by its column's name
step1.text: Setting a cell keeps the original value beside the new one and marks the row Modified. The record set knows nothing of compositions, only that one column of one row now differs from what was read.

step2.title: Add and delete in place
step2.text: An added row is Added and has no originals. A deleted row stays in the table, marked Deleted, with its originals, because the write-back needs them to find the stored row; an added row deleted again simply goes.

step3.title: Write back one row at a time
step3.text: The adapter takes the changed rows in table order and builds each statement from the column names: an insert for an Added row, and for the others an update or a delete that applies only where every stored column still equals the row's original. Statements sent so far: {sent}.

step4.title: Accept or refuse each row
step4.text: A statement that finds its row is accepted: the stored row takes the new values and the row's originals become its current ones, or the row leaves the set if it was deleted. One that finds nothing is refused, and {refusal}. Rows refused so far: {refused}.

pseudocode.ordinary:
fill(query):
  table = store.select(query)            # columns by name, rows by id
  for row in table:
    row.state = Unchanged
    row.original = copy(row.current)     # the values read

set(row, column, value):
  row.current[column] = value            # the original stays beside it
  if row.state is Unchanged: row.state = Modified

add(values):
  table.append(state: Added, current: values, original: none)
delete(row):
  if row.state is Added: table.remove(row)
  else: row.state = Deleted              # kept, with its originals

writeBack(table):
  for row in table where row.state is not Unchanged:
    statement = statementFor(row)        # insert, or update or delete where every column equals row.original
    matched = store.run(statement)       # a write of its own

    if matched: accept(row)              # originals = current, Unchanged; a deleted row leaves
    else if continueOnError: row.refused = true
    else: stop                           # the rows after this one stay unsent

item0.relevance: This app's actor board renders the uifa-board-v1 response that the app's own API serves, and board.ts declares that response's panels, sections, rows and cells.
item0.explanation: The author's reading of the code, not a claim that it was designed as this pattern: BoardStore fetches the whole response with one GET through BoardApi and keeps it as one value that the page reads until a refresh fetches it again, so the board holds a disconnected copy of the projection it was served. Each Row holds its Cells, and every cell carries its own column key, label and status, the metadata a query result carries about its columns; BoardRow hands those cells to DotlnKeyValueList, which draws any row from its cells' labels without knowing what kind of row it is, the data-aware screen the pattern was made for. The facade indexes the same rows and cells by key to resolve links. It stops at reading: the contract is lossy and read-only, rows keep no state and no original values, nothing is written back, and a refresh replaces the whole document.

item1.relevance: ADO.NET is the data-access layer of .NET. Its DataSet is a disconnected record set supplied by the platform, and its DataAdapter both fills one and writes its changes back.
item1.explanation: Update looks at each changed row and runs the adapter's insert, update or delete command for it. A row removed from a DataTable is simply gone, leaving the stored row alone, while a deleted row stays in the table marked for deletion, so that Update can delete the stored one. The documentation's update command finds its row through the column's Original value, since the Current one may have changed, and a command that reports no row affected is taken as a concurrency conflict. AcceptChanges runs for each row as Update processes it, overwriting the row's Original values with its Current ones. Setting ContinueUpdateOnError lets the caller read each failure from the RowError of the row concerned once the update is over, and the order of inserts, updates and deletes is left to the caller, who can pass the rows of one state at a time.

item2.relevance: Spring's JDBC support returns a query result as an SqlRowSet from JdbcTemplate.queryForRowSet: a record set in Java's own terms, and the nearest public match for what the board does with its response.
item2.explanation: The interface mirrors JDBC's RowSet as a disconnected variant of a result: a reader moves through the rows with next, previous, first, last and absolute, reads a cell by column label or by index, and asks getMetaData for the number, types and properties of the columns. It throws Spring's own unchecked InvalidResultSetAccessException instead of SQLException, and it is Serializable, with implementations, which typically hold disconnected data, asked to be serialisable as far as they can. It declares no method that changes a row: like the board's response it is a record set for reading, and a change has to be written by other means.

limits.item0: Without a transaction round it, the write-back is only as atomic as one row. Set the saves by another tab to 1 and step to the end: the note of Screen the wood is already stored when the update of Hold the bridge finds nothing, the adapter stops, and the deletion of Cross the ford and the new Dawn raid are never sent. Let it go on past a refused row as well and the store takes every change but the rename, leaving that row marked for someone to resolve by hand.
limits.item1: Every original column guards the write, not only the one that changed. The other tab changed only the note of Hold the bridge and this session only its title, yet the update compares both originals and is refused. Comparing only the changed columns would let both edits through, which is right here and wrong wherever two columns must agree.
limits.item2: Column names are the interface. The record set and the adapter find cells by the names the query returned, so a renamed or misspelt column shows itself only when a row is read or written. The board carries the same risk in its cells' keys: a link naming a key that the next projection renames becomes an unavailable target on the page, and no compiler warns of it.
limits.item3: A table is flat. A composition's steps and trials are lists inside it, which a record set can hold only as further tables keyed back to the composition or as a column of opaque text it cannot check; the closer the data is to a tree, the harder the tabular shape works against it.

item1.why: The fill and the write-back in this example are a gateway's work: one object per table that runs its queries and hands back record sets. Read it for the statements behind the adapter.

intuition.text: Think of a registry as an address rather than an object: code asks for a service by name and is handed whichever instance belongs to the place that code runs in. Two callers asking under the same name may receive one object or two, and nothing in their own code says which; the registry's scope decides. That is why choosing the scope, not writing the lookup, is the design work.
intuition.situation: In this app the Tools home, the catalog page and the soldier scene all read the catalog. Threading the loader from page to page would put it into every route and component; instead each page asks for it under one key, and where the routes register it decides who shares. The two Tools pages read through one loader and its cache, while the scene has a loader of its own.

example.name: One catalog key, three pages
example.description: The Tools home, the catalog page and the soldier scene each need the catalog loader, and none is handed it: each asks for it under one key, as the app's catalog store and facades do with inject(CatalogToken). {scoping} The reader opens the Tools home, then the catalog page, then the scene, and comes back to the catalog page from the scene; return visits: {returns}.

step0.title: Register a factory in a scope
step0.text: A registration pairs a key with the factory that can build its object, and lives in a scope: a route's providers, or a page's own when each page registers it. Nothing is built yet.

step1.title: Build on the first lookup, then share
step1.text: A lookup finds the key in the caller's scope. The first lookup there builds a loader and keeps it, and every later lookup in that scope is handed the same one. Lookups so far: {lookups}; loaders built: {built}.

step2.title: Read through what was handed
step2.text: A page reads the catalog through the loader it received. Each loader reads once and answers later reads from its cache, so pages that share a loader share its read. Reads so far: {reads}.

step3.title: Close with the scope
step3.text: A page's own providers close when the page does and take their loader with them, while a route's registration stays for the next visit. A page that reopens with a scope of its own therefore builds and reads again.

pseudocode.ordinary:
provide(scope, key, factory):
  scope.entries[key] = { factory, held: none }

lookup(scope, key):
  entry = scope.entries[key]
  if entry is missing: refuse "nothing is registered under key"
  if entry.held is none: entry.held = entry.factory()
  return entry.held

read(loader):
  if loader.cache is empty:
    loader.cache = fetch the catalog
  return loader.cache

closePage(page):
  if page has a scope of its own:
    discard page.scope and everything it holds

item0.relevance: The key under which this app's Tools pages and soldier scene find the catalog loader, the bundled reader of every work's rows and studies.
item0.explanation: The author's reading of the code, not a claim that it was designed as this pattern: CatalogStore, ToolsFacade and SceneFacade each call inject(CatalogToken) rather than receiving a loader as an argument, so the token is the well-known key and Angular's injector is the object that answers. provideCatalog, in catalog-loader.ts, registers the factory, and where it is listed sets the scope: tools.routes.ts lists it once for the Tools home and the catalog page, with a comment that both pages then read and persist the same state, and provideSceneFeature lists it again, so the scene gets a loader of its own. The catalog test kit registers a fake that records its calls through the same provideCatalog. It stops short of a classic registry in that the injector is configured from outside and answers inject() only in an injection context, such as while a class is being created, so nothing reaches it through a static method from anywhere, and a missing registration shows only when the lookup runs.

item1.relevance: Spring's transaction support keeps the resources of the running transaction, such as its JDBC connection, in this class, and data-access code finds them there instead of being passed them.
item1.explanation: It is a registry with static methods whose data is scoped to the thread: each piece of state is a ThreadLocal, and resources sit in a per-thread map keyed, usually, by the factory that produced them, so getResource, given a data source, finds the connection resource bound to this thread. bindResource refuses a second value for a key already bound and unbindResource removes one, and the class comment leaves binding to the transaction managers while resource code only looks up. Since version 7.0, bindSynchronizedResource also unbinds the value when the transaction completes and restores whatever it replaced, and clear() resets the thread's registered synchronisations and transaction attributes.

item2.relevance: MikroORM is a TypeScript object-relational mapper; RequestContext is how code serving one HTTP request finds that request's own entity manager, and with it the request's identity map and unit of work.
item2.explanation: create forks the entity manager and runs the handler inside an AsyncLocalStorage store, so the scope is one request's chain of asynchronous calls, JavaScript's nearest equivalent of a thread, and the static getEntityManager is the lookup. The global entity manager's getContext, after any transaction context, asks the configured context resolver, RequestContext.getEntityManager by default, so code holding the global instance still works on its request's fork; and since allowGlobalContext is false by default, using the global instance for context-specific work outside any request context throws rather than letting requests share one identity map. Where AsyncLocalStorage is missing, the async context falls back to a single variable and logs a warning: the same lookup, with its scope widened to the whole process.

limits.item0: Choosing the scope is the decision, and a wrong choice fails quietly. Set each Tools page to register its own and step to the return: the catalog page no longer shares the home's loader, so it builds another, every return visit builds one more and reads the catalog again, and since provideCatalog also provides CatalogStore, each page would hold its own copy of the reading state. Too wide a scope fails the other way, handing one caller's object to callers it does not belong to.
limits.item1: The lookup hides the dependency. A class that calls inject(CatalogToken) shows no catalog in its constructor's signature, so nothing at compile time says that it needs one; placed under a route that registers none, it fails only when the lookup runs, with Angular's no-provider error.
limits.item2: A lookup works only where the registry can be reached. Angular resolves inject() only in an injection context, such as while a class is being created; a lookup from a later callback or timer throws, so a class that needs the loader later has to take it at construction and keep it.
limits.item3: A registry kept by hand in a module variable lasts as long as the module does. A spec that puts a stub into one has to put the original back, or the next spec in the same file reads the stub. The app's test kits avoid this by registering fakes as providers, as provideCatalogTestKit does through provideCatalog, so the fake lives in the injector its test builds.

intuition.text: Objects written to work inside one program ask each other many small questions: the board for its panels, a panel for its rows, a row for its cells. In memory each question is nearly free; across a network each one waits for a round trip and carries its own headers, checks and chance of failing. A remote facade puts one broad operation at the network's edge. The client calls it once, and behind it, inside the server's process, the facade asks all the small questions itself and copies the answers into one reply. That reply cannot be the server's objects, which live in its memory and point at one another, so it is a Data Transfer Object, a copy made for the trip. This is why the two patterns come as a pair: the facade decides how much one call does, and the transfer object is what that call carries in and out.
intuition.situation: The actor board opens and must show five panels drawn from different sources. If the app's API served one object per call, the page would ask for the panel list, then each panel, then each row, before it could draw anything. Behind a facade the page asks once and draws when the reply lands. The facade is also the one place where the caller is checked for the whole board, and where a source that fails can become a panel marked unavailable instead of an error that takes the board with it.

example.name: One call for the whole board
example.description: The board page needs the five panels of the recorded board: Actors with {rowsActors} rows, Builds with {rowsBuilds}, Mechanisms with {rowsMechanisms}, Work with {rowsWork} and Blueprint with {rowsBlueprint}. Behind the app's /uifa-board-v1 route the author places a facade, loadBoard, over sources that serve one object per call. {buildsSource} The facade is the author's sketch of the app's own API: in this repository the route is answered by a mock that serves a recorded copy of the board.

step0.title: Take one coarse call
step0.text: The page sends a single call for the whole board. The facade checks once that the caller may read it, a check every panel shares, and lists the panels with a call to the sources in its own process.

step1.title: Make the small calls locally
step1.text: For each panel the facade calls the panel's source, then each of its rows, inside the server's process, where a call costs no round trip. Local calls so far: {localCalls}; a page calling one object at a time would have sent {oneByOneCalls} across the network for the same panels. The facade only calls and copies: any rule about what a panel shows stays with the sources.

step2.title: Keep a failed part a part
step2.text: When a source cannot be read, the facade writes that panel into its response as unavailable, with the reason, and reads on. A facade that lets the failure escape ends the call instead, and the panels it had already read are lost with it.

step3.title: Answer once, keep nothing
step3.text: The facade returns its response as the one reply and keeps nothing for the next call. Read one object at a time, the same board would take {boardCalls} calls across the network, and even with each round's calls sent together it would take {rounds} rounds, since the panel ids come from the list and the row ids from each panel.

pseudocode.ordinary:
loadBoard(caller):
  require caller may read the board
  response = { viewModelVersion: "uifa-board-v1", panels: [] }
  ids = sources.panelIds()

  for id in ids:
    try:
      panel = sources.panel(id)   // readPanel
      rows = [sources.row(rowId) for rowId in panel.rowIds]
      response.panels.add({ id, status: "available", rows: copyOf(rows) })

    catch failure:
      if not reportsFailures: raise failure
      response.panels.add({ id, status: "unavailable", explanation: failure.reason })   // reportUnavailable

  return response

item1.project: eShopOnContainers · the web shopping aggregator's BasketController
item1.relevance: Microsoft's reference microservices application for .NET puts a backend-for-frontend aggregator between its web client and its services, and the aggregator's controllers are remote facades in all but name.
item1.explanation: UpdateAllBasketAsync takes one request carrying every basket line, reads the current basket from the basket service and every product it names from the catalogue service in one batch, merges them, saves the basket once and returns the whole basket as one object. The controller is marked [Authorize], so the caller is checked once, at the facade. Two things depart from a thin facade: the calls behind it are remote too, gRPC calls to the basket and catalogue services, so it moves the chatter onto the network between services rather than into one process; and it merges duplicate lines by product and sums their quantities, a rule a thin facade would leave to the basket service.

item2.project: Azure Architecture Center · Gateway Aggregation pattern
item2.relevance: Microsoft's cloud architecture guidance describes the same move for microservices: a gateway that takes one client request, calls several back ends and returns one combined response.
item2.explanation: It argues from the same cost, a client sending, awaiting and handling many requests over a high-latency network, and adds the decision this study's failure case turns on: when one back-end call times out or fails, the gateway may return a partial response or fail the whole request, and the guidance asks for that choice to be made explicit so that clients can predict it. It also advises keeping the aggregation to light composition and shaping, with custom domain logic or long orchestration in a service behind the gateway.

item1.supports: The book itself (Addison-Wesley, 2002), where Remote Facade belongs to chapter 15, Distribution Patterns. This study names the chapter and quotes nothing from it.

limits.item0: One call shares one fate. Set the Builds source down to 1 and the reporting to 0, then step to the end: the Builds read fails, the facade stops, the panels it had read are thrown away and the page shows only its load-failed notice, although a page that called each panel itself would still have drawn the others. With reporting on, Builds travels as an unavailable panel, which is what uifa-board-v1's section status and explanation are for, and the client must then draw that state.
limits.item1: Coarse cuts both ways. The board's one call brings all {totalRows} rows although the page shows one panel at a time, and a refresh reloads the whole board. A facade shaped for each screen grows a method for every new view; one shaped too broadly sends what nobody reads. Its operations should follow what clients do, not the objects behind them.
limits.item2: The facade is the easy place to add a rule, such as hiding actors with no evidence, because every call passes through it. A rule there is missed by every other way into the sources and copied by the next facade; keep the facade to checking, calling and copying, and keep the rule in the domain behind it.
limits.item3: Inside one process it is pure cost: copying into a response and serialising it buys nothing when the caller could call the sources directly, and a facade that keeps a client's state between calls ties that client to one server. It earns its place only at a network boundary, which the first law of distributed object design argues against drawing at all.

item0.why: The other half of the pair. The facade sets how much one call does; the transfer object is what that call takes and returns. Read it for how the board's reply is shaped, versioned and checked by the page.

item1.why: Where the operations the facade calls belong, with their rules. Go there when the question is what the application does; the facade only offers it across a network.

item2.why: The case for needing no facade: keep the objects in one process. Go there before drawing the network boundary a facade would then have to cover.

intuition.text: Most of what an application does for its users is a short list of things it can be asked: save this, open that, load the other. Each of those involves several parts working in a set order: a read, a rule, a write, and telling whoever is watching. A service layer gives each such request one operation, and every kind of client calls that operation instead of repeating the steps, so the order, the rules it asks for and the write it guards are written once and are the same for everyone who asks.
intuition.situation: The soldier scene saves a composition from its Save button, and an import box could save one from an exported file. If each had its own save code, the import's copy is the likely one to forget that another tab may have saved since the page opened, and to write over that tab's work. One saveComposition for both keeps the fresh read, the scene check and the order of writing and telling in one place.

example.name: Three saves through one operation
example.description: Browser storage holds two compositions, Flank left as composition-{flankId} and Hold the ridge as composition-{ridgeId}, and two tabs of the soldier scene have both listed them. The Save button in tab A saves Night march; then the Save button in tab B saves Dawn raid; then the import box in tab A takes River crossing, {importFile}. {importRoute}

step0.title: Clients hold no workflow
step0.text: The Save button and the import box each call saveComposition with the composition they hold. Neither reads storage, gives an id or tells a list anything: that is the operation's job, so both kinds of client get the same steps in the same order.

step1.title: The domain holds the rules
step1.text: domain.check refuses a composition exported from another scene and gives an accepted one the id one past the highest stored. So Night march takes the id after composition-{ridgeId}, though the ids between composition-{flankId} and composition-{ridgeId} are free: a gap left by a composition that could not be read is never filled again.

step2.title: Read afresh, then ask
step2.text: saveComposition reads the list from storage on every call, never the copy its tab holds, so a save made in the other tab meanwhile is part of what it extends. It hands that list to the domain; a refusal ends the operation with nothing written and nothing announced.

step3.title: One write
step3.text: The list as read, plus the accepted composition, goes to storage in a single setItem, so storage holds either the old list or the new one, never part of each. Writes so far: {writes}.

step4.title: Announce after the write
step4.text: Only when the write has succeeded does the service tell the tab's listeners, its saved list among them, and it tells them once. The other tab hears nothing: it sees the new list the next time its own saveComposition reads storage.

item0.relevance: The scene page's facade holds the soldier scene's save and open operations; it is the nearest the app comes to a service operation, though only one page calls it.
item0.explanation: The author's reading of the code, not a claim that it was designed as this pattern: save() is an operation script. It does nothing for an empty run, reads storage again because another tab may have saved and a save writes the whole list (except after a failed save, when the list in memory is the only copy), builds the composition with the id one past the highest, and dispatches compositionSaved. The scene store adds it to the list and its persisted state writes the list in that same change, flagging a failed write instead of undoing it. open(id) and importJson(text) both end in one private #open, so two entry points share one workflow. It stops short of a service layer in three ways: the scene page is its only client, the id and title rules sit in the facade file rather than with the composition, and because the write happens as the store reacts to the event, save cannot tell its caller whether it succeeded. The one place where two of the app's pages share an operation is the catalog store, whose summary load answers both the Tools home and the catalog page.

item1.relevance: PetClinic is the Spring project's sample application in its classic layered form, and ClinicServiceImpl is the one service its web controllers call; the class comment calls it a facade for all of them.
item1.explanation: Every method forwards to a repository, so this is a service layer as a domain facade, with hardly any workflow of its own. What it adds is the boundary: reads are declared @Transactional(readOnly = true), saves @Transactional, and findVets is @Cacheable, so transaction and cache policy is set once at the service rather than in each controller. VetController shows several clients in miniature: one call to findVets feeds the HTML page, the JSON list and the XML list. One method, findVisitsByPetId, carries no transaction annotation, a reminder that a boundary declared method by method is only as complete as each declaration; and because Spring applies the annotations through a proxy, one service method calling another on the same object gets no transaction of its own.

item2.relevance: eShopOnWeb is Microsoft's reference ASP.NET Core application on Entity Framework Core; its operations live in services in an ApplicationCore project beneath the web pages.
item2.explanation: CreateOrderAsync is an operation script: it loads the basket with its items, guards against a missing or empty basket, loads the catalog items the basket names, builds order items from them and adds the order through a repository. The repository base class it uses saves changes on every add, update and delete, so each service call is a save of its own. That shows a boundary drawn too fine: the checkout page calls SetQuantities, then CreateOrderAsync, then DeleteBasketAsync, three operations and three saves, so the workflow of a checkout lives in the page, and a failure after the order is added leaves the basket behind.

item0.title: Service Layer, in Martin Fowler's online catalog of the book's patterns
item0.supports: The pattern's name, its attribution to Randy Stafford, and its short statement: a layer of services that sets the application's boundary, defining the operations available to client layers and coordinating the application's response to each, so that several interfaces do not each repeat that coordination.

item1.title: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture, the publisher's page
item1.supports: The book itself (Addison-Wesley, 2002), where Service Layer, by Randy Stafford, belongs to chapter 9, Domain Logic Patterns. This study names the chapter and quotes nothing from it.

limits.item0: A service layer protects only the clients that call it. Set Imports that skip saveComposition to 1 and step to the end: the import box writes the list tab A holds, which was read before tab B saved, so Dawn raid is gone from storage while tab B still lists it, and River crossing takes the id tab B gave Dawn raid. No list is told about River crossing, so it shows nowhere until a reload.
limits.item1: The fresh read narrows the gap but does not close it. saveComposition reads, checks and only then writes the list it read plus one; a save that lands between its read and its write is lost all the same. Closing that needs a check at the write itself, such as a version compared when the list is written, which the service gives one place to but does not supply.
limits.item2: A rule is only as safe as the path that asks for it. Set Exports from another scene to 1 with the import calling saveComposition: the domain refuses River crossing and nothing is written. Set both inputs to 1 and the import's own code writes the foreign export into storage, because the scene rule lives in the domain and only the service asks it.
limits.item3: Announcing after the write lets a list lag storage. Tab B's list does not show Night march until tab B's own saveComposition next reads storage, so a client that needs to know at once must ask. The app's scene store takes the other order: it adds a saved composition to its list as the event arrives, writes in the same change, and when the write fails keeps the composition on screen with a notice that it will not survive a reload.

item0.why: Each operation of a service layer can be a transaction script, as saveComposition nearly is; read it when the rules are so few that the scripts are the whole of the logic and no domain is worth separating.

item1.why: Read it for where the rules go when domain.check grows into objects with behaviour of their own; the service then shrinks to the coordinating steps above them.

item2.why: A service layer is called in process, one fine operation at a time. Read it when those operations must be offered across a network, where each call is costly and the interface has to be coarse.

item3.why: Read it for what a remote client sends and receives in place of the domain's own objects, once the service's operations are called from outside the process.

item4.why: Read it when the question is which screen comes after a save rather than what the save does: that flow sits above the service, not inside it.

intuition.text: A test should fail only when the code under test is wrong. A real service makes tests fail for reasons of its own: it is down, slow or rate-limited, and it cannot be told to refuse, drop a connection or stall on cue. A service stub takes the service's place for the length of a test and answers from memory at once, so the code around it, the gateway's translation included, runs exactly as in production while the answers become the test's to choose.
intuition.situation: The board store has to show a refusal, a lost connection and a timeout as well as the board itself. The app's own board API is not built yet, and even a live one could not be asked to answer 503 or to stall for just long enough. The store's spec needs each of those answers on demand, in milliseconds, and the same on every run.

example.name: The board store's four cases, against a stub
example.description: Four of the cases the board store's spec runs go through the board gateway, with the app's HTTP API replaced by a stub that answers in memory: the recorded board, a refusal with status {refusalStatus}, a dropped connection, and a timeout staged by holding the answer {stubDelayMs} ms against a case limit of {timeoutMs} ms. {stubKind} The stub's board is contract version {fixtureVersion}; at release one call goes to the live API, which serves version {liveVersion}.

step0.title: Put the stub where the service was
step0.text: The spec points the gateway at the stub instead of the API. The gateway's front and back are the production code; only what answers them has changed, so whatever the cases learn about translation holds for the real thing.

step1.title: Let each case choose its answer
step1.text: A dynamic stub reads the scenario each case writes on its request and answers in the API's own terms: a status and a board, a refusal, a dropped connection, or an answer held back. A static stub ignores the scenario and has one answer for everyone, the recorded board.

step2.title: Translate as in production
step2.text: The gateway waits for the stub's answer and translates it exactly as it would the API's. The timeout case costs only its own limit, {timeoutMs} ms, because the stub holds its answer for {stubDelayMs} ms, longer than the case will wait.

step3.title: Assert in the app's terms
step3.text: Each case compares what the store holds with what it expects. Passed so far: {passed}; failed: {failed}; waited on the stub: {waited} ms; calls to the live API: {liveCalls}.

step4.title: Meet the live service once
step4.text: At release the recorded case's request goes to the live API. Only that case can run there, since the live API will not refuse, drop or stall on request. If its contract has moved on since the stub's board was recorded, the case that passed against the stub fails now.

pseudocode.ordinary:
spec.setup():
  gateway.api = stub          // the front and the back are unchanged

stub.answer(request):
  if the stub is static: return ok(recordedBoard)
  match request.scenario:
    refusal: return refuse(refusalStatus, unavailableBoard)
    network: return dropConnection()
    timeout: return after(stubDelayMs, ok(recordedBoard))
    none: return ok(recordedBoard)

case.run():
  request = { scenario: case.scenario }
  outcome = gateway.load(request, limit: case.timeoutMs)

case.assert():
  if outcome == case.expected: passed
  else: failed

release():
  gateway.api = liveApi
  outcome = gateway.load({ scenario: none })
  recordedCase.assert(outcome)   // the other cases cannot be staged live

item0.project: DotLn-Angular · boardHandlers, the MSW stand-in for the board API
item0.relevance: This app's board has no live API yet, so boardHandlers answers GET */api/uifa-board-v1 in memory, through Mock Service Worker, for the specs, the browser tests and local play.
item0.explanation: The author's reading of the code, not a claim that it was designed as this pattern: with no scenario header the handler is a static stub that returns the recorded board; the x-dotln-test-scenario header makes it dynamic, so unavailable returns the unavailable projection, refusal the same projection with status 503, failure a 500, network a transport error, and timeout the board after a 200-millisecond delay, longer than the 30-millisecond limit the store's spec sets for that case. Specs add the header with an extra interceptor and the browser tests with an extra HTTP header, so each request carries its own answer and nothing chosen for one case carries over to the next. Where it stops: it stands in for the network, below HttpClient, rather than behind the gateway's interface, so BoardApi and the interceptors run for real; it records nothing, unlike the app's in-memory storage kit, which keeps every write; and npm run check:fixtures holds its canned boards to the pinned uifa-board-v1 schema, which guards against a fixture leaving the contract but not against a live service moving to a new one.

item1.relevance: Angular's testing backend takes the place of HttpBackend, the back of Angular's own HTTP client, so a spec runs HttpClient and its interceptors against a stub that never touches the network; it is the stub most Angular specs use where this app uses MSW.
item1.explanation: The class serves both as the HttpBackend and as the HttpTestingController a spec injects. Its handle method answers nothing by itself: it queues each request as an open TestRequest, and the spec finds it with expectOne or match and flushes the answer it wants, which makes it a dynamic stub whose answers are chosen request by request. verify fails the spec if any request is still open, so the stub also checks that nothing unexpected was asked.

item2.project: Rails · Action Mailer's test delivery method
item2.relevance: Rails mailers hand each message to a configurable delivery method, and the test method is the stub a new Rails application's test environment selects, so no test sends real mail.
item2.explanation: DeliveryMethods registers four methods by name, SMTP, file, sendmail and test, and wraps each mail with the class the configured name points to, so swapping the real service for the stub is one setting. The test method is Mail::TestMailer, which sends nothing and keeps every mail it is given in a list that ActionMailer::Base.deliveries exposes: a static stub that records its calls, so a test asserts on what would have been sent rather than on a mailbox.

item0.title: Service Stub, in Martin Fowler's online catalog of the book's patterns
item0.supports: The pattern's name, its attribution to David Rice, and its short statement: tests that depend on outside services the team does not control become slow and unreliable, and replacing such a service while testing with a local, in-memory stand-in removes that dependence.

item1.title: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture, the publisher's page
item1.supports: The book itself (Addison-Wesley, 2002), where Service Stub, by David Rice, belongs to chapter 18, Base Patterns. This study names the chapter and quotes nothing from it.

limits.item0: A static stub tests the happy path only. Set the stub to static and run the suite: every request gets the recorded board, so the refusal, lost-connection and timeout cases fail, not because the store is wrong but because the stub cannot say anything else. The failure paths need a stub the test can steer.
limits.item1: A stub is a recording, and recordings age. Set the live API's version to 2: every case still passes against the stub, and the first call to the live API fails, because the stub still serves the contract it was recorded from. Holding the fixture to a pinned schema, as this app does, catches a fixture that leaves the contract, not a service that moves to a new one; only a check against the service itself does that.
limits.item2: A staged timeout holds only while the stub outwaits the case. The timeout case passes because the stub holds its answer for {stubDelayMs} ms and the case stops waiting after {timeoutMs} ms; give the case a limit longer than the stub's delay and the board arrives in time, so the case fails. In this app the two numbers live in two files, the handler and the store's spec, and nothing ties them together.
limits.item3: A stub at the wrong seam tests the wrong code. One put in place of the gateway's front hands the store finished outcomes and skips the translation these cases exist to check; one put at the network, as here, runs the gateway for real but must speak the API's raw terms, its statuses, bodies and failures, exactly as the API does, and so grows into a second implementation of the API that nothing checks against the first.

item0.why: The stub needs a seam to stand behind; read it for where the gateway's front ends and the back a stub replaces begins. Its study follows one of these requests to the real API.

item1.why: To choose between the stub and the real service by configuration rather than code, as the app's environment files switch its mock worker on for development and off for production.

item2.why: To declare the interface the stub and the real service both implement where the client owns it, so swapping one for the other changes no caller; the app's StorageToken and CatalogToken work that way, and their test kits are stubs that record calls.

item3.why: When what is swapped is a repository's storage, an in-memory collection in place of the database, rather than a remote service behind a gateway.

intuition.text: Write the page as it will look and leave a named gap wherever a value goes. Read from top to bottom, the file is then the page: its order, its headings and the place of every value can be seen without following any code. Filling the gaps is the easy part, and any template engine does it; what the pattern really settles is who decides what. Whatever the helper works out reaches the page as a plain value, which a test can check by calling a function. Whatever the template works out for itself, which fragment to show and which to leave out, is code living in markup, and the only way to test it is to render the page.
intuition.situation: The catalog shows every concept study, of every work, through one Angular template, study.html. Unit of Work, a movement study and a messaging study all come out of that file; what differs is the StudyView it is handed, which mapStudy builds from the record, the drawing's selected moment and the loaded catalog. To make a study look different, an engineer edits the template; to make it say something different, the record or the helper. Each new requirement raises the question the pattern turns on: is this a value the helper should hand over, or a decision the template should make?

example.name: The Unit of Work reading, from study.html
example.description: A reader opens Unit of Work in the catalog. The Tools facade loads its record and its model, and mapStudy builds one StudyView for the moment the drawing opens on. study.html, the file every study uses, then fills its markers from that view: the authored line, the example's name, the intuition and its situation, the figure with the states drawing, the closed explanations, the nearby concepts and the closing line that names the reviewers. Nothing in the template knows it is showing Unit of Work: handed another study's view, it shows that study.

step0.title: Write the page with markers
step0.text: study.html is markup holding three kinds of marker. An interpolation or a property binding places one value of the view, such as the example's name. The t pipe places a message from the catalog and fills that message's own markers from named values, as the authored line takes its author and its date. The control-flow blocks, @if, @switch and @for, keep, choose or repeat a fragment. The page has no words of its own: the app's template check refuses rendered text that does not pass through the t pipe, apart from the view's already translated text inside an element marked translate="no".

step1.title: Prepare the values in the helper
step1.text: Before any marker is filled, mapStudy turns the record, the drawing's selected moment and the loaded catalog into one StudyView. It fills the record's prose from that moment's values, keeps only the nearby concepts the catalog holds, finds the work's next study and sets the drawing to null when the record has none or no model is loaded. The template binds the view once, as vm; besides it, the template reads only the link builder it is given and the list of explanations its component derives from the same view.

step2.title: Fill each value marker
step2.text: Each interpolation and each t pipe is replaced by its value, in page order: the authored line, the example's name, the intuition and the situation. Angular compiles these markers into code before the page runs and, with strict templates on, checks each against StudyView's type, so a marker naming a field the helper does not supply fails the build rather than the page. When the reader steps the drawing, the helper builds a new view, and only the markers whose values changed are written again.

step3.title: Keep or choose a fragment
step3.text: @if on vm.visual keeps the figure only when the helper supplied a drawing. For Unit of Work it did, and @switch on the drawing's family puts in the states drawing, a case this batch adds after the commit the link above pins, rather than the flow, marble or movement one; a record with no drawing gets null from the helper, and the whole figure is left out. Inside the figure the template starts to decide for itself: it tests a drawing's family together with whether it has a second drawing to choose whether to offer two views, and together with the selected view to choose which guide to print under the legend.

step4.title: Repeat a fragment for each item
step4.text: @for over vm.nearby writes one list item for each nearby concept, with its link, its title and the reason to read it, and @for over the sections writes one disclosure per explanation, with the RxJS one only for a study that has such a reading. Neither loop filters anything: the helper has already decided what each list holds, so the template only repeats. The nearby list has no empty case, so a view with no nearby concepts would leave its heading over nothing.

pseudocode.ordinary:

item0.relevance: This app's catalog shows every concept study through one Angular template, study.html, which fills its markers from the StudyView that mapStudy builds for the reading.
item0.explanation: The author's reading of the code, not a claim that it was designed as this pattern: study.html is markup and markers and nothing more. Its interpolations and t pipes place values and messages from one view, bound once as vm, and the app's template check refuses rendered text that bypasses the t pipe, so even the page's fixed words live in the message catalog. The helper is mapStudy, a pure function with a spec of its own, which fills the record's placeholders, drops nearby concepts the catalog lacks and returns a null drawing when there is none, so the conditions round the figure and the next-study link only ask whether a value is there. The pattern stops in two places. The template still decides some things for itself, testing a drawing's family together with its second drawing or its selected view to choose the view switch and the guide under the legend. And it is not a page anyone can open as it stands: Angular compiles the markers into code and, each time the reader steps the drawing, updates only the values that changed, where the pattern's page is filled once for each request.

item1.relevance: Rails is the Ruby web framework, and Action View is its view layer. Its ERB templates are this pattern with embedded code as the markers, run by a view object that mixes in Rails' helper modules.
item1.explanation: ActionView::Base documents the two ERB markers. Ruby between <% and %> runs and writes nothing, which is where loops and conditionals go; the value of the expression between <%= and %> is written into the page. The view object includes the helper modules and, when it is created, copies each value it is handed as an assign onto itself as an instance variable, so a template reads @people and calls a helper by name. Each template is compiled to a method and recompiled during development when its file changes. Shared fragments are sub-templates, written into a page with render and handed local variables, and a locals magic comment in a template restricts which locals it accepts, which gives the template a declared list of the values it takes.

item2.relevance: Thymeleaf is a server-side Java template engine with official integration for Spring MVC. Its markers are attributes on ordinary HTML elements, and the engine is built round keeping a template usable as a design prototype that opens in a browser as it stands: the designer's side of this pattern built into the engine.
item2.explanation: StandardTextTagProcessor is what th:text runs. In an HTML template it evaluates the attribute's expression, turns a null result into empty text, escapes it and replaces the element's whole body with the result. So the sample text a designer types inside the element, which a browser shows when the file is opened as it stands, exists only in the prototype, and rendering discards it for the real value. The marker is an attribute that browsers ignore rather than code in the markup, which keeps the file a page; the price is a second copy of every value, the sample, that nothing keeps in step with the real one.

item0.title: Template View, in Martin Fowler's online catalog of the book's patterns
item0.supports: The pattern's name and its short statement: information rendered into HTML through markers placed in an otherwise static page, which resolve into calls that gather the dynamic content. The page points to chapter 14 for the full treatment.

item1.title: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture, the publisher's page
item1.supports: The book itself (Addison-Wesley, 2002), where Template View belongs to chapter 14, Web Presentation Patterns. This study names the chapter and quotes nothing from it.

limits.item0: Logic arrives one condition at a time, and splits a decision as it comes. When a reader switches a movement study to its chart, the helper swaps the legend for the chart's series, but the template swaps the caption for the chart guide itself, by testing the drawing's family and view; switching a messaging study to its marbles has the helper swap both. The same choice now lives in two files, and the template's half is tested only by rendering the page.
limits.item1: A marker outside any conditional prints whatever the helper hands it, an empty string included. The closing line places the reviewers as one joined string, and a draft names none, so a draft's page reads ‘Reviewed by .’ before the rest of the sentence. The template needs a branch for that case, or the helper a different message; the studies check keeps a record with fewer than two reviewers from shipping, but not from being shown while it is a draft.
limits.item2: What a marker shows when its value is missing depends on the kind of marker. A placeholder in a message passed through the t pipe becomes an empty string when no value of its name is given, unless a message happens to share that name; a placeholder in a record's prose that the selected moment does not supply stays on the page as written; a message key missing from the catalog throws during development and shows the key itself in production. Reading the template alone, no one can tell whether a gap will show as nothing, as a placeholder's name or as an error.
limits.item3: The template is not a page a designer can open. The pattern's promise is a file that reads as the page it makes; study.html is markup threaded with @if, @switch and @for blocks and pipes that only Angular's compiler turns into a page, so changing its layout is a developer's job. The app takes a different benefit instead: strict templates check every marker against StudyView when the app builds, which a page whose markers are resolved only as it renders cannot do.

item0.why: The object the template reads every value from, here the StudyView that mapStudy returns. Read it for how much a helper should prepare, since each decision it leaves out lands in the template.

item1.why: Where the page's shape follows the data's, as when the input is already a tree, a program that walks the data and writes each element's markup fits better than a fixed page with gaps. Read it for the other way of producing the same HTML.

item2.why: When many pages must share one look, a first stage builds a logical page from the data and a second turns it into HTML, so a change of look is made once; one template per page cannot promise that. Read it before copying the same markup into a second template.

item3.why: The template only shows; something has to take the request, gather what the page needs and hand the helper over. Read it for that half of a page, which in this app happens in the Tools facade before the template sees anything.

intuition.text: Organise the code by what is asked of it rather than by the things it handles. Each request a user can make has a procedure of its own, and to know what an import does you read the import's procedure from top to bottom: the order of its checks, what a refusal does, what it changes. The data passing through are plain records with no behaviour of their own, and a check two requests share is a helper both call, so reuse comes from calling, not from belonging. To an engineer used to reducers and pure helpers this is the familiar shape of an Angular feature: a facade method or an effect for each intent, pure functions for what they share. Its weakness mirrors its strength: a rule binds only the scripts that remember to call it.
intuition.situation: In the soldier scene an operator pastes a composition that someone else exported, to replay it on their own screen. One procedure takes the text, makes sure it is an export, checks the composition's fields and every one of its steps, makes sure it was made in this scene, and then opens it or tells the operator it could not. When a report says an import failed, a colleague reads that procedure and the helpers it calls, and nothing else.

example.name: Importing an exported composition
example.description: The operator pastes exported text into the soldier scene's import box. The import script parses it, checks that it carries the export tag, calls the shared checks on the composition's fields and on every step, checks that it was made in this scene, and replays it from its own seed. When the page loads, a second script reads the saved list back from browser storage and calls the same shared checks on each composition, but not the scene check.

step0.title: One procedure for the request
step0.text: importJson is the only code a paste runs through. It asks parseExport for a composition, raises the page's import-failed flag when there is none and otherwise opens it, so reading those few lines is reading the whole request.

step1.title: Check the envelope and the scene
step1.text: parseExport refuses text that does not parse or lacks the export tag, calls the shared check on the composition, and then asks the one question only an import asks: was it made in this scene? Every refusal is the same quiet null.

step2.title: Factor the shared checks into helpers
step2.text: isComposition checks the type of every field and calls isStep on every step, which holds the step to the engine's last frame and to its bounds on parameters. Both are pure functions over plain data: the rule belongs to whoever calls it, not to the composition.

step3.title: Reuse by calling
step3.text: The reload is a second script. When the page loads, restoreStoredScene reads the saved list back from browser storage and keeps each composition that isComposition accepts, so the field and step rules are written once. It runs no scene check, because that rule lives in parseExport, which the reload never calls.

step4.title: Act on the scene
step4.text: open sets the run's seed to the composition's and puts the field back to its first frame with the steps scheduled; the engine applies each when its frame comes and refuses one of a kind it does not run, or one with no units to act on. The composition stays plain data the whole way: nothing it holds can check or replay itself.

pseudocode.ordinary:
importJson(text):                      // one procedure for one request
  composition = parseExport(text, scene.id)
  importFailed = (composition is null)
  if composition: open(composition)

parseExport(text, sceneId):
  value = parseJson(text), or return null if it does not parse
  if value.schema != exportSchema: return null
  c = value.composition
  if not isComposition(c): return null
  if c.sceneId != sceneId: return null   // only the import asks this
  return c

isComposition(c):                      // shared by the import and the reload
  id, title and sceneId are non-empty text, seed is a whole number,
  note is text, every kept trial has its fields,
  and every step passes isStep
isStep(s):
  s.at is a count no later than lastFrame, toolId and kind are non-empty,
  and every parameter is within largestNumber of zero and not below its least value

restoreStoredScene(stored):            // the reload, a second script
  if stored is not the current stored shape: return nothing
  keep each c in stored.compositions where isComposition(c)
  // no scene check: that rule lives in parseExport, which this script never calls

open(composition):
  seed = composition.seed
  rewind the field to its first frame with composition.steps scheduled
  // the engine applies each step when its frame comes, refusing an unknown kind
  // or a step with no units to act on

item0.relevance: SceneFacade is the soldier scene's single entry point for what the page asks of it: applying a tool, setting an objective, and saving, opening, exporting and importing a composition.
item0.explanation: The author's reading of the code, not a claim that it was designed as this pattern: save, open, exportJson and importJson are each one method for one request, read top to bottom. importJson hands the pasted text to parseExport in stored-scene.ts, whose shared checks, isComposition and isStep, the store also calls through restoreStoredScene when the page reloads, so the field and step rules are subprocedures reused by calling; the scene check is parseExport's own and binds imports alone. The cousin stops short of the pattern at the write: no method writes storage itself. save dispatches an event, SceneStore's reducer appends the composition, and withPersistedState writes the whole list when the save count moves, so the store, not the script, decides when data reaches browser storage.

item1.relevance: Spring is an application framework for Java services, and TransactionTemplate is its programmatic way to run one block of code inside one database transaction: the frame a transaction script is written in.
item1.explanation: execute takes a callback, which is the script, asks the configured transaction manager for a transaction, runs the callback with the transaction's status and commits when it returns. A runtime exception or an error from the callback rolls the transaction back and is thrown on; any other exception also rolls it back and comes out wrapped. The class's documentation describes the intended split: data-access code that knows nothing of transactions, called from inside a service's callback, so the service alone marks where the transaction starts and ends. What it adds to the pattern is that boundary: the script says what to do, and the template makes sure all of it commits or none of it does.

item2.relevance: Doctrine DBAL is the database layer under Doctrine ORM and a separate library in its own right: it runs SQL and inserts, updates and deletes rows by table name and arrays of columns, with no objects in between. That makes it the thin gateway a PHP transaction script talks to.
item2.explanation: transactional runs a closure, the script, between beginTransaction and commit and passes it the connection. If the closure throws, the transaction is rolled back and the exception goes on; if the commit itself fails it rolls back as well, except after a few failures, a deadlock or a constraint violation among them, where it issues no rollback of its own. A script that calls a subprocedure which opens its own transaction does not start a second one: in this version a nested call becomes a savepoint inside the outer transaction, so shared steps can be factored out without breaking the request's all-or-nothing write.

limits.item0: A rule that every request should obey is obeyed only by the scripts that call it. Here the scene check sits on the import's path alone: when the page loads, the reload accepts any well-formed composition from browser storage, whatever scene it names. That is harmless while one scene writes the dotln-angular.scene key; a second scene sharing that key would need the check added to the reload by hand, and nothing in the code points to the gap.
limits.item1: Closing such a gap means handing the rule what it needs from every caller. The reload runs inside SceneStore's persistence options, which never see the scene definition, so moving the scene check into isComposition would first mean threading the scene's id into the store; each such difference between requests adds another argument to a shared helper.
limits.item2: Rules that differ by kind become branches in every script that has to know. The engine's refusalOf already asks whether a step is the objective kind to decide whether it needs units; each new kind with a rule of its own adds a branch there and in any other procedure that must agree, which is where one class per kind starts to pay for itself.
limits.item3: Each script carries its own share of the care the store needs. Because a save writes the whole list, the save script reads browser storage again before appending, in case another tab has saved since; a new script that writes the list and forgets that read would silently drop the other tab's compositions.

item0.why: The same import with each rule owned by the composition, the step or the scene. Read the two side by side, and go there when rules start to differ by kind of step or must bind every path a composition takes.

item1.why: A set of scripts behind one interface is a service layer of the operation-script kind. Go there to decide which requests the facade offers and where each one's transaction begins.

item2.why: The thin gateway a script calls to reach a whole table. The app's nearest is withPersistedState's read and write of one storage key; go there when scripts start repeating their storage calls.

item3.why: When the scripts work one record at a time, an object per stored row with its own find and update keeps the storage calls out of the script while leaving every rule in it.

intuition.text: A business transaction often changes several objects before any of it should reach the store. Rather than writing each change as it happens, one object keeps three lists, of what was created, what was changed and what was deleted, and at the end writes all of them in a single transaction, or nothing at all.
intuition.situation: The soldier scene saves a composition today by adding it to a stored list. Suppose it also let the operator rename and delete saved compositions: in one session they create one, rename another and delete a third, then save. The save should carry all three changes together, so storage never holds a library where the rename landed but the deletion did not, and two renames should cost one write, not two.

example.name: One save for three changes
example.description: Two compositions are stored: Flank left at version {versionFlank} and Hold the ridge at version {versionRidge}. In one session the operator creates Night march, renames Hold the ridge {renames} times and deletes Flank left, then saves once. {rival}

step0.title: Read objects clean
step0.text: Objects read from the store start in no register. The unit notes the version each was read at, because the commit checks it.

step1.title: Register what is new
step1.text: A created object joins the new register. Nothing is written: it has no row until the commit inserts one.

step2.title: Register a change once
step2.text: A changed object joins the dirty register the first time it changes. A second change finds it already there, so two renames still mean one update.

step3.title: Register what is deleted
step3.text: A deleted object moves to the removed register and stays stored until the commit. A new object deleted before the commit is simply forgotten.

step4.title: Commit in one call
step4.text: The commit opens one transaction, inserts the new objects, updates the dirty ones and deletes the removed ones, each update and delete only where the stored version is still the one read. One mismatch rolls the whole call back. Store calls so far: {calls}; written at once: {immediateCalls}.

pseudocode.ordinary:
load(ids):
  for id in ids:
    row = store.read(id)
    held[id] = { title: row.title, version: row.version }

registerNew(object):
  held[object.id] = object
  newObjects.add(object.id)

registerDirty(object):
  if object.id in newObjects or object.id in dirty:
    return
  dirty.add(object.id)

registerRemoved(object):
  if object.id in newObjects:
    newObjects.remove(object.id)
    return
  dirty.remove(object.id)
  removed.add(object.id)

commit():
  call = store.begin()
  for id in newObjects: call.insert(held[id])
  for id in dirty: call.update(held[id], expected: held[id].version)
  for id in removed: call.delete(id, expected: held[id].version)
  if call.versionMismatch(): call.rollback(); return refused
  call.commit()
  newObjects.clear(); dirty.clear(); removed.clear()

item0.relevance: This app's soldier scene keeps the operator's saved compositions in SceneStore, the nearest thing the app has to a unit of work.
item0.explanation: The author's reading of the code, not a claim that it was designed as this pattern: the store changes its compositions in memory as events arrive, and withPersistedState writes the whole list to browser storage only when the save counter moves (writeOn: state.saves), so one save is one write. Just before it, SceneFacade.save re-reads the stored list, because another tab may have saved since, and appends the new composition. It keeps no registers and checks no versions; that is safe today only because a save adds a composition and never changes or removes one, which is where a unit of work, and the version check of an optimistic lock, would come in.

item1.relevance: Doctrine is the PHP object-relational mapper behind Symfony's usual persistence layer, and its UnitOfWork class is this pattern under its own name.
item1.explanation: Each managed entity has a state: new, managed, removed or detached. At commit it first computes change sets by comparing every managed entity with what it read, so code need not register a change by hand. It then opens one database transaction, runs inserts first so that new rows exist before anything refers to them, updates in a fixed order to lower the risk of deadlocks, deletions last, and rolls back if any step fails.

item2.relevance: MikroORM is a TypeScript object-relational mapper whose entity manager is built round a unit of work and an identity map.
item2.explanation: persist and remove put entities into a persist set and a remove set. commit computes change sets for everything managed, groups them by kind and writes them inside one transaction where the database supports it. A commit that starts while another is running waits in a queue until the first finishes.

item3.relevance: Hibernate ORM is a Java object-relational mapper that implements Jakarta Persistence; each session keeps an ActionQueue, which is where its unit of work's lists live.
item3.explanation: The queue holds a session's insertions, updates and deletions in separate lists until a flush, then runs them in a fixed order: orphan removals, inserts, updates, the collections' changes and deletions last, so new rows exist before anything points at them. Before it runs anything it refuses a flush in which a stored object refers to one that was never saved, and with insert ordering switched on it sorts the inserts by what they depend on.

limits.item0: A unit of work kept open for a long session holds the versions it read at the start. Set the saves by another tab to 1 and step to the commit: Hold the ridge is stored at a newer version than the one held here, so the whole save is refused, and the creation and the deletion are lost with the rename unless the operator makes them again.
limits.item1: Nothing coordinates two units of work. Each tab's unit checks only the versions it read and knows nothing of the other's registers, so they meet only at the store's version check; without that check the later commit silently overwrites the earlier one.
limits.item2: It writes only what it is told about. An object changed without registerDirty is never written. Frameworks such as Doctrine close that gap by comparing every managed object with what they read, at the cost of that comparison on every commit.
limits.item3: The commit has to order its statements. A new object that refers to another new one must be inserted after it, and a deleted object must go after the rows that point at it; a unit that ignores those dependencies fails on the store's foreign keys.

item0.why: To know that two lookups of one row are the same object, so that a change made through one copy is not lost to another. A unit of work usually keeps one.

item1.why: The commit calls a mapper to turn each registered object into its row; read it to see what writing one object involves.

item2.why: An object filled in later still has to join the unit when it changes; read it for how a ghost becomes an object the unit tracks.

item3.why: The version check at commit is this lock; read it for what to do when the check fails.
